subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 195, to amend the Surplus Crown Assets Act.
He said: In my opinion this is a bill of no great importance. It is a tidying up bill. In June, 1944, the house passed the Surplus Crown Assets Act to set up a corporation to dispose of surplus war materials. The corporation was formed and it has carried out its work. It has sold goods producing a gross revenue to the crown of $462 million. The disposal of war equipment surplus as a result of the war is pretty well finished, but the corporation is still receiving declarations of surpluses at the rate of about 280 a month from various departments, and from the armed services. The corporation controls a good deal of real estate acquired during the war, which it has not yet been able to sell, and it still has to collect some $31 million of accounts outstanding. It is quite obvious that the corporation must carry on for a considerable period, but it does not need all the machinery that was used when it was carrying out its war duties.
The purpose of the bill is to simplify the corporation, to dispense with the crown assets allocation committee, which is required by the present act, and to streamline the act to allow it to carry out its duties to the extent that is required under present-day conditions.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
On clause 1-Definitions.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have one or two questions to ask. I shall first of all be a bit critical because the public accounts committee was not set up this session to give us an opportunity to call witnesses in connection with the War Assets Corporation. The procedure and practices of the corporation were criticized by the Auditor General in the report of March 31, 1949, in which he said:
I have examined the accounts of War Assets Corporation for the year ended March 31, 1949, and have obtained all the information and explanations I have required. The procedures and practices of the corporation were not of such a nature as to permit establishing by examination of records maintained that all assets received for disposal had been fully accounted for.
There is another matter that I should like to bring to the attention of the committee. Why cannot the Canadian Commercial Corporation look after the selling of these surplus assets as well as do the buying? It has an organization already set up. It is true that in industry there is a purchasing department and a sales department, but they more or less deal with the commodities of one industry. Here we have to purchase for eighteen departments or more, and it would seem reasonable that the sale of surplus goods could be handled by the same agencies. In industry the products are related, but in this instance the products are unrelated and cover a wide range of articles. I feel that it would be better business, and the government would do a better job, if it were handled by one government agency, and if the buying and selling were done under the one head.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext: That is not the experience of the department. The buying is one job, and selling the vast accumulation of unrelated products is another job. At one time the War Assets Corporation had over ten thousand employees located in all parts of the country Its staff has been reduced to about 169 employees today, and the volume of work is decreasing; nevertheless the new sales that will be made in this current year represent a return to the crown of some $11 million. It is big business, business for a staff that is specialized and used to evaluating the kind of second-hand material that this corporation deals with. That is totally different from the experience required by the staff of the purchasing corporation.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext:
This first clause does some of the things which the minister referred to when he outlined the purpose of this bill. For example, it gets rid of the surplus crown assets allocation committee and makes one or two other administrative changes. I see, Mr. Chairman, that you are looking at the clause and trying to see where these things are.

If you take this clause and compare it with the section of the bill for which it is a substitute you will find that it leaves out such an important part of the machinery as the surplus crown assets allocation committee. If the purpose of the bill is, as the minister indicated, simply to tidy up the work of surplus war assets, it would seem reasonable to eliminate some of the machinery and get things on a more simplified basis. On the other hand, as indicated by subparagraph (b) of this clause and the other clause to which it refers, the name of the organization is being changed. The word "war" is being left out and it is being made to appear as a more permanent organization. In fact, the minister has just said that there are still 280 declarations of surplus per month.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext:
It does look as though this body will stay in existence for some time. As a matter of fact the very change in the name makes me wonder whether, instead of its being an organization merely for the disposal of surplus war assets, it is becoming an organization that can dispose of crown property at any time and on any terms.
That being so, I confess frankly-although the minister may be able to set aside my fears-that there are one or two things which concern me. Section 1 (e), when compared with the corresponding paragraph in the original act, gets rid of the necessity of orders in council in certain cases. The minister is aware of that; I need not read it. In other words this bill puts more power directly in the hands of the minister himself.
The minister has already said that this bill gets rid of the crown assets allocation committee. Formerly there were three bodies connected with this matter, namely, the corporation, the committee and the minister. The committee was a body to advise the minister. Now the committee will be gone, with just the minister and the corporation remaining. And later on we shall find that the minister has power to delegate his authority to the corporation.
As I say, all this is reasonable, if this job is just about over, or if it is a case of just tidying up. But if what we have here is the setting up of a peacetime crown assets disposal organization, it seems to me we should ask why the necessity for orders in council is being done away with, and why more power is being put in the hands of the minister, and this minister in particular. I have other questions relating to other sections.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext: This is intended to be a permanent disposal organization.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext:
It is permanent?
Surplus Crown Assets Act

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext:
Yes, permanent. Prior to the war there was a disposal agency centred in the Department of Finance; but in effect each department of government had its own disposal arrangements, subject to the approval of the disposal officer.
The problem has grown a good deal with the years. As I say, the war itself has created problems which will be with us for many years, collections being made representing some $31 million. Some of these payments are not due for several years. The government has decided to make the surplus crown assets disposal agency a permanent instrument of government; and this bill is for that purpose.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext:
That being so, I feel I should press my question as to why a change has been made doing away with the necessity for orders in council in certain cases before property can be declared as surplus crown assets.
Section 2(f) of the act, of which section 2(e) in the bill is the amending section, states:
(f) "surplus crown assets" means property that has been
(i)	included in a report made to the minister under section three; or
(ii)	declared by the governor in council to be unnecessary to satisfy the requirements of the government department by which it is kept, administered or controlled; and
has not been subsequently deleted from the report with the consent of the minister or disposed of pursuant to the provisions of this act.
The new subsection 1 in the bill before us amends section 2 of the act by getting rid of paragraph (f) and substituting the new paragraph (e) which reads as follows:
(e) "surplus crown asets" means the property that is included in a report made to the minister under section three and has not subsequently been deleted from the report with the authority of the minister or disposed of pursuant to this act.
The principal difference between those two paragraphs is the elimination of the necessity under certain circumstances for orders in council in order that goods be declared surplus. Would the minister tell me why the orders in council are being done away with and why greater power is being placed in the minister's hands?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext: I think my hon. friend has overlooked one word.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext: The word "or"?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext:
Yes, the word "or". As a matter of fact all the surplus has been declared on the report made to the minister under section 3. We have never used orders in council to declare surplus, and it is not necessary under the old act. Departments could do it that way if they wished; but it

Surplus Crown Assets Act was so much simpler to do it the other way that that is the way we always followed. And since declaration by the governor in council has never been used in the past, there is no use perpetuating the method.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext: The minister may not always see eye to eye with me, and he may think I always want to fight with him, but I accept that as a satisfactory answer-

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext: -even though there seems to be some amazement at my doing so. Another question has to do with paragraph (c) in the amending bill in which a number of crown corporations or other bodies are exempted from the definition of "government department". I notice that the Polymer Corporation is not mentioned here. Is there any significance in that omission?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION

No. The corporations mentioned are self-contained corporations owning their own assets, and the sale of whose assets would normally go into the funds of the corporation concerned rather than into those of the receiver general. My hon. friend will appreciate that all the moneys recovered by crown assets corporations are paid over to the receiver general. However, in the case of the Canadian National Railways, the railway is a separate corporation and would naturally recover funds arising from disposal of its property. May I say, Mr. Chairman, that I believe I have overlooked a duty-and I hope the committee will bear with me in my omission. subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION

That section 1 of the bill be amended by adding the words "or the National Harbours Board" immediately after these figures "1937" in line 21 at page 1 of the bill.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext: I hope my hon. friend will not tell me I am breaking the rules-because I think I am.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext:
I have no objection to the amendment. What I have to say can be said

now as well as back on the clause, so may I return to the point I raised earlier, using Polymer Corporation as an example.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext: This section repeals sections 5, 6, 7 and 8 of the original act and does away with the crown assets allocation committee, which formerly advised the minister in connection with these matters. Why does the minister feel that that committee is no longer necessary?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext: In the early days of disposal certain assets that were declared surplus by one department could be used by another department and the purpose of the crown assets allocation committee was to make sure that there was not a use within the government for articles declared surplus. Further advice on the procedures is not necessary as the procedures are well established. The work of the crown assets allocation committee had dwindled to the point where no one would attend its meetings because there is nothing of interest going on. This results from a definite change in the character of the assets being declared surplus.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION
speechtext: It is all being left to the minister.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION

Surplus Crown Assets Act Soulanges canals. The department has outstanding leases on properties and it was not thought well to disturb operations that have an historical background.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION

(b) approve the transfer of surplus crown assets from one government department to another, subject to such terms and conditions as he may consider desirable.

If it is required, it can be transferred by ministerial action without calling the board together.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS CROWN ASSETS BY CROWN ASSETS DISPOSAL CORPORATION

I have another question on this clause Paragraph (e) is being reworded to read:
(e) authorize a government department to dispose of surplus crown assets in such manner, upon such terms and subject to such conditions as he may consider desirable.

Gold Mining
Here again it is the Minister of Trade and Commerce who may do this. The old paragraph read:
(e) empower a government department to sell surplus crown assets upon such terms and subject to such conditions as he may consider desirable.
The section is being changed so that the minister may approve of the disposal of surplus crown assets in such manner as he may consider desirable. Does that mean that things may now be given away rather than sold?

DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE 413. Departmental administration, $468,107.
Will the Minister of Trade and Commerce make a statement to the house on the international situation with respect to trade and commerce as it affects Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is customary from time to time for the Minister of Trade and Commerce to discuss the present economic situation and forecast the future. I have been doing both every year since 1944, and in the process I have been accused of being Canada's No. 1 optimist. However, at the moment I have no particular regrets about any statement I have made throughout that period. The statement I am going to make now represents, in my opinion and that of the officers of the Department of Trade and Commerce, a fair estimate of the situation we are facing today and expect to face during the next calendar year.
The Canadian trade picture for 1949 has, on balance, been favourable. While there has been some decline in sales to traditional markets, Canada's exports in terms of dollars will be about as high as last year, while imports will be slightly higher. In a period of readjustment following the abnormal conditions of the last decade, we have been able to maintain our export trade at an extremely high level and to dispose of our major surpluses. The necessary adjustments so far have been made without any real dislocation of Canadian industry; in fact the general level
Supply-Trade and Commerce of economic activity in the country as a whole has continued to improve. The year 1949 has been a prosperous one for Canada, and national production, income, employment and consumption will be higher than last year. The strong domestic market that has developed from our recent industrial expansion and high level of domestic prosperity has been an important factor in offsetting to some extent the loss of overseas markets. For example, exports of motor vehicles have been reduced sharply with exports this year at some $40 million below 1947. Yet the home market is now absorbing close to the maximum output of this industry, with the increase in domestic sales about double the fall in exports. In cotton textiles and in electrical equipment the story is similar.
Our exports are a major factor today as they always have been in the past, and Canada's prosperity is dependent to a large extent on the state of world trade and more particularly on our trade with the United Kingdom and the United States, our two largest suppliers as well as our two largest customers. I should like to deal first with these two countries before going on to some of the broader issues of international trade.
During the past year a concerted effort has been made by the Canadian government, as well as that of the United Kingdom, to help Britain and the rest of the sterling area earn enough dollars to remain large-scale customers for Canadian goods. Because of the lack of other sources of dollar revenue that were available in pre-war years, these countries depend more and more on their direct sales to dollar countries to pay for their imports from those countries. In other words, the United Kingdom's exports both to Canada and to the United States have become a most important determinant of what she can afford to buy in these two countries. The success of the measures taken to increase our imports from Britain is apparent from the trade figures. In 1947 our exports to the United Kingdom exceeded our imports from there by $564 million. In 1949 the deficit on merchandise trade will be reduced to about $375 million. For the sterling area as a whole, the gap will have been cut by over 40 per cent.
In terms of dollars, the increase in our purchases from the United Kingdom has been substantial. In 1946 we were importing about $140 million worth of goods. Imports for 1949 should be in excess of $300 million. While some of the rise has been due to price changes, there has also been a definite increase in volume. In relation to our population, I think these figures are significant. During the past year, on a per capita basis, we were

Supply-Trade and Commerce buying British goods at the rate of $24 for every person in Canada. The comparable figure for the United States is only $1.40.
Turning now to our trade with the United States, we find that our imports from that country have been increasing, an indication of the continuing high level of business activity in our own country. The unbalance in our trade is not, however, as great as it was in 1947. In that year the unfavourable balance amounted to nearly $1 billion. In 1949 our adverse merchandise balance will be larger than last year but will only be about half the 1947 figure. Increased exports to the United States have played an important part in improving our American trade picture. Nevertheless an excess of imports over exports amounting to $500 million is a matter of some concern and creates a problem for us. In 1949 over 70 per cent of our import requirements came from the United States.
I think we will all agree that a high level of imports is an essential part of Canadian foreign trade. This does not exclude the possibility of increased Canadian production in a number of items. In recent years we have found that we are able to produce many goods that we had formerly imported. At the same time a very large volume of imports is necessary to maintain the flow of raw materials to our factories, to help provide the building materials and machinery and equipment for our record investment program, and to satisfy the high demands of the Canadian consumer. A substantial volume of imports is associated with a high level of prosperity in this country. We are therefore interested from the point of view of our exchange and dollar problems, not in reducing the amount of our imports, nor necessarily increasing it, but in changing the source from which some of these goods are obtained.
We have attempted by every means at our disposal to accomplish the necessary adjustments in our external trade balances by means which will expand the total volume of our trade. I have on many occasions explained that Canada's trade policy is to sell more to the United States and to buy more from the United Kingdom and other European countries. There is an important aspect of this policy which I wish to stress, and which is of great importance to domestic industry in Canada. It is no part of our policy to increase over-all imports as such. Canada's normal level of imports is sufficient to provide the outside world with enough Canadian dollars to buy our exportable goods. What we need is a redirection of our trade so that we shall approach closer to a balanced position both with the dollar countries and with the sterling area.

Our own position in this regard may perhaps be explained most clearly by contrasting it with that of the United States. Much has been said in recent weeks by our friends in the United States about the traditional lack of balance between their exports and their imports. It is their avowed intention for the future to accept a higher level of imports from other countries so that the outside world can afford to buy their goods. There is no counterpart of this problem in the Canadian situation. Our problem, to repeat, is one of redirecting our trade to achieve better regional balances. If we could buy more of the commodities we need from the sterling area and from the countries of western Europe, the benefits would be twofold. First, we would improve our United States balance of trade; second, we would help our non-dollar customers to earn more dollars with which to maintain their purchases of Canadian products. A better bilateral balance in our trade with individual countries would help to stabilize Canada's exports.
During the past year, Canada has participated in a number of international efforts to deal with the problem of world trade. Together with thirty-two other nations at Annecy we took part in the second round of negotiations under the general agreement on tariffs and trade. The concessions gained, as they become effective, help to improve our trade with a number of countries in such commodities as wheat, forest products, hides and leather goods, codfish, aluminum, lamps. As you know, the three major trading countries of the world met last September in Washington. As a result of these discussions, the foundation has been laid for a co-operative approach to our mutual problems on the part of the United Kingdom, the United States and ourselves. One important development has been the American government's firm stand in support of increased imports into the United States and the need to get rid of the obstacles that now exist. Only recently, Canadian officials took part in discussions on specific difficulties in customs administration, which were a followup of the tripartite talks.
In the period that lies immediately ahead, numerous changes may take place in our foreign trade as well as on the home front. Individual exporters are already encountering difficulties. We are, however, in a strong position to meet any adjustments that may be necessary in our economic life. The Canadian economy is operating at an exceptionally high level. It is a flexible economy, and can adjust itself to new situations.

Canada has the resources, the equipment, and the skills needed to produce goods that are needed in the markets of the world.
By any standard, 1949 has been a good year, and the outlook for 1950 is also good. It is too early to forecast, with any degree of accuracy, the general level of activity that will prevail in 1950, but there is every reason to believe that it will be not very different from 1949. We can, of course, look forward to some falling off in foreign trade totals. There will probably be some easing of price, coupled with some reduction in physical volume. Agricultural crops are, on the whole, lower this year. For example, wheat is down from 393 million bushels last year to an estimated 367 million bushels this year; oats from 359 million bushels to 316 million bushels; and barley from 155 million bushels to 120 million bushels. Agricultural items bulk large in our trade totals. However, assuming a continuation of a satisfactory level of general business activity in the United States, it is a' reasonable expectation that we shall be able to continue to dispose of the surpluses of our primary production.
It must be acknowledged that our exports of a variety of manufactured products will be reduced but, as in the year 1949, this should in most cases be offset by the continuing high domestic demand.
The other main pillar of the Canadian economy is capital investment, and here again, while it is too early to forecast in terms of dollars, it is clear that capital investment will continue at a high level-probably not much different from that of 1949. To realize the truth of this, one has only to think of the tremendous investment now being undertaken in connection with western oil, and the transportation of that oil; of the extension of iron ore operations in Steep Rock and of the plans for the development of Labrador iron ore, the beginning of which may well take place next year. Then there is the continuation of the very substantial development of hydroelectric projects in various parts of Canada; the titanium development in Quebec, as well as public projects such as the trans-Canada highway. Some adjustments will undoubtedly have to be made; some production patterns may have to be altered, but the underlying strength of the two main pillars of our welfare-exports and domestic investment-show promise of a satisfactory level of employment and income in Canada in 1950.

I listened with interest to the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I hope that the prophecies that he has made will be fulfilled next year. While we can point out with some justification that
Supply-Trade and Commerce our world trade position is satisfactory now, nevertheless I feel that our trading position is anything but satisfactory to certain sections of our population.
The problem Great Britain and the other sterling areas have in attempting to reduce dollar purchases has resulted in a severe reduction in the sale of many Canadian commodities to Great Britain and other European countries. That reduction in markets will be felt most keenly by certain segments of our population. We do know we are finding it increasingly difficult to maintain markets in Great Britain for fish products, timber and tobacco. I do not wish to deal with those matters at length, because I feel that there are many members in the house who are better qualified to discuss those particular aspects of our trade position than I am.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

I am sure the committee listened intently to the statement given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon. I am glad that the minister is still optimistic about our trade situation for the coming year, but I am afraid that that optimism cannot be shared to the same extent by large sections of the Canadian people. We do know that at the present time we are finding difficulty in marketing many Canadian products. The timber industry is finding difficulty because Great Britain is short of dollars with which to purchase her normal supply of timber. We know that the fishing industry is having difficulty at the present time in marketing its products. We know that the tobacco industry has lost the British market to a very large extent. Statistics show that within the first eight months of the year 1947 exports of flue-cured tobacco from Canada to Great Britain amounted to eighteen million pounds; but for the same period of this year the export of flue-cured tobacco has dropped to eight and a half million pounds.
Mr. Chairman, I am sure my hon. friend wants to be accurate. Exports this year are $8,500,000.

I will accept the minister's correction, but I can tell him that I got my figures from the dominion bureau of statistics publication on Canadian exports and I was very careful to check for their accuracy. It spoke about pounds in the first eight months of this year.

I am sorry; perhaps the hon. member is right.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
If the minister knows he is right I will accept it.

I was giving the figure for the full year. I noticed that the hon. member mentioned only the first eight months. I daresay the figure for the full year would be twice the amount he mentioned. The price of flue-cured tobacco is about 50 cents a pound. I daresay the hon. member's figures are correct for the first eight months.

The first eight months of 1947 and the first eight months of 1949.
This afternoon the minister made the statement that he was reasonably sure Canada could dispose of surplus agricultural products in 1950. I hope he is correct. I think he and the Minister of Agriculture should have conferred because the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture at the FAO conference would lead anyone to believe that he feels that indeed Canada is facing a very grave situation in respect to markets for agricultural products. I shall quote from page 2 of the speech of the Minister of Agriculture, which reads as follows:
Our monetary difficulties today threaten to reproduce the situation which existed twenty years ago; a lack of that free movement of food from those with food to spare to those in want . . .
Again:
We, in turn, must find some other natural markets for these products or shrink our production of them because the United Kingdom has not the dollars with which to buy.
All through the speech he spoke of increasing agricultural difficulties. Certainly the Minister of Agriculture has in mind the fact that today Canada has large surpluses of many agricultural commodities, and we may indeed face great difficulties in trying to obtain markets for them.
The situation in respect to agricultural products is not greatly different from the situation in respect to timber and fish products. I saw a report in tonight's Ottawa Journal from Pembroke, Ontario, which read:
The Canadian Splint and Lumber Corporation, one of Pembroke's largest industries, will be forced to close down on Friday, December 16, because of the British dollar shortage, the Journal learned today.
Therefore we are indeed facing grave difficulties in finding markets for many of our products. We have difficulty in finding markets for apples. We know that we have a surplus of cheese, and according to press reports while we may expect a contract with Great Britain for another fifty million pounds of cheese next year, the price will be reduced from thirty cents a pound to between twenty-five cents and twenty-seven cents a pound.

We know that we have on hand in Canada a huge quantity of evaporated milk for which there is no adequate market.
I do not feel that in the future we can look with any surety to the United States taking our surplus products. According to figures published by the United States Department of Agriculture, in 1947 the United States farmers had a net income of $18 billion. The net income of United States farmers is running at approximately $14 billion for the present year, so it would appear that there is likely to be a drop in agricultural income in the United States within that two-year period of some 22 per cent. If the United States farmers are having difficulty maintaining their net income, surely we cannot have any real expectation of being able to market increased quantities of agricultural products in the United States in the future. Already we have observed a trend in which the prices of agricultural commodities in Canada are dropping.
The Canadian index for farm products was 263-9 in August, 1948. That index has dropped to 249-3 in September of this year, a drop of 14-6 within that time.
I believe that markets for livestock and dairy products are essential for more reasons than keeping the farmers' income high. An adequate market for livestock and dairy products means that farmers can engage in diversified agriculture, and diversified agriculture is necessary if we are to maintain agriculture on a permanent basis, and if we are to maintain the fertility of our soil. But while we are facing a surplus of some livestock and dairy products and while I do not believe that we are facing an imminent surplus of grain, nevertheless in the grain situation throughout the world there is already apparent a trend which should lead us to give this matter a great deal of consideration.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce quoted the crop yields for this year. It seemed to me that he was taking some satisfaction from the fact that we had reduced yields of our various grains because it would likely prevent a surplus appearing with which the government would have to deal. If we look at our carryover stocks of grain we find that the carryover of wheat was 98-7 million bushels, 21 million bushels higher than the year before.
Mr. Chairman, I am sure my hon. friend wishes to be accurate. What did he say the carryover of wheat was last year?
I said 98-7 million.

He is entirely mistaken. I do not mind his quoting the party line, ascribing

motives and talking of depressions and one thing and another, but I do wish he would be accurate in his figures.
These figures were taken from the quarterly statement on grain, issued by the dominion bureau of statistics.
It is not true. They are not correct.

I shall give the committee the figures as I have them, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce can correct me where they are wrong. The carryover of wheat was 21 million bushels larger this year than at the same period a year ago. The carryover of oats was 59-1 million bushels as compared with 47-9 million bushels a year ago, an increase of 11-2 million bushels. The carryover of barley was 29 million bushels, a decrease of 2-4 million bushels; the carryover of flax was 10-7 million bushels, an increase of 7-3 million from the year before; the carryover of rye was 12 million bushels, an increase of 11-1 million from the year before.
The general picture with regard to our carryover on July 31 of this year in relation to our carryover of grains a year ago was that while our carryover did not constitute a huge surplus, nevertheless it was above the average as compared with the year before.
If we are going to have adequate markets for grain, then the British market in that regard is most important. The domestic policy the British are following in relation to the production of grain in that country is certainly of vital interest to the farmers of Canada. The British are following a policy of producing more and more of their own food at home. I hope the minister will accept these figures, because they were taken from a United Kingdom information office publication.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
I shall take it for granted that the figures he has given are correct. Has he any remedy or suggestion to offer to correct the situation?
I am glad the hon. member has asked that question, and I shall answer it later.
Yes, in about an hour.

Do not be so impatient. Great Britain is increasing agricultural production at home. In the year 1948-49 she produced 37 per cent, by calories, of the food she consumed, as compared with 31 per cent pre-war. Bread-grain production in Great Britain in
Supply-Trade and Commerce 1948-49 was 44 per cent above the pre-war figure. Her production of other grains was 98 per cent above pre-war.
So in addition to an increase in the carryover of grains in Canada we find Great Britain increasing her own production of grain. Along with that she has undertaken bilateral agreements with other countries for the purchase of large quantities of grain. For example a year ago she signed a bilateral agreement with the U.S.S.R. for the purchase of 750,000 tons of coarse grains. According to a speech made in February by Mr. Harold Wilson, president of the British board of trade, the U.S.S.R. delivered that quantity on time -indeed delivered a quantity slightly in excess of the 750,000 tons. A press report since that time tells us that Great Britain has entered into a bilateral agreement with Russia for the purchase this year of a million tons of coarse grains.
In addition to the bilateral agreements Britain is making for the purchase of coarse grains outside Canada, the countries of Europe taken together are importing less grain now than they did pre-war. May I quote to the Minister of Trade and Commerce one paragraph from page 29 of the FAO publication entitled "World Commodity Problems": Europe, which normally took 90 per cent or more of the world coarse grain exports, took less than 7 million tons in the past two years as compared to 11 million tons before the war. Stocks of coarse grains in the four export countries were 24 million tons larger than a year earlier.
Thus Europe is now taking greatly reduced quantities of grain as compared with the quantities purchased before the war. The chief exporting countries have had on hand this year 24 million tons of coarse grain more than they had on hand a year ago. The United States does not provide us with a market for increased quantities of grain, in my opinion, since in that country they have a large carryover.
According to an article in the Christian Science Monitor of September 15, stocks of corn in the United States amounted to 550 million bushels and stocks of wheat to 150 million bushels. We find an increased average carryover of all grains in Canada this year, with Great Britain increasing her domestic production of grain and entering into bilateral agreements for the purchase of grain from countries other than Canada. We find too Europe is now buying less grain than she did before the war.
If this trend continues I am fearful lest we may have a surplus of grain in this country in the not too distant future. The farmers are interested in knowing at the earliest possible moment what the government's policy is going to be for the 1950 crop

Supply-Trade and Commerce in relation to wheat prices, and the prices of oats and barley. The Canadian wheat board operates under the Minister of Trade and Commerce. There has been a five-year pool with an initial price now paid to producers of $1.75 a bushel. Throughout a large part of that period our farmers were selling wheat to be processed into flour and baked into bread to be sold in Canada for less than the amount our wheat was bringing in many other countries of the world.
During part of that period we were selling large quantities of wheat to Britain at prices less than those at which we were selling wheat to other countries. Farmers feel they have made a real sacrifice during that five-year pool. Nevertheless they have welcomed the pool. They believe in stability and they are now asking that the government maintain the wheat board legislation and that they be given another pool period. I would hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce can maintain the same initial price next year. In view of the sacrifices our farmers have made I say they should be guaranteed the present initial price for another five-year pool period.
We come now to the government policy in relation to coarse grains. We know that year in and year out farmers have advocated the closing of the grain exchange, and have advocated that the wheat board handle oats and barley in exactly the same way it handles wheat. Certainly in June, when the announcement was made, farmers believed that oats and barley would be handled by the wheat board and would be completely taken off the speculative market. They were disappointed to find that while the wheat board is the sole buying agency for oats and barley, the grain exchange is still being used in the sale of oats and barley.
The Saskatchewan wheat pool convention meeting at Regina in November, according to an article appearing in the Leader-Post on November 7, passed a resolution asking the federal government to place oats and barley under the wheat board in exactly the same position as wheat. That resolution was passed unanimously.
I would suggest that when the Minister of Trade and Commerce is deciding upon an initial price for oats and barley next year he should keep in mind establishing a price which bears a fair relationship to the initial price for wheat. At my own elevator point the farmer gets an initial price for the wheat he delivers of $1.58J per bushel, but for barley he receives only 67 cents and a fraction per bushel. Those initial prices do not bear reasonable relationship one to the other.

I believe the initial price of barley should be two-thirds the initial price of wheat, while the initial price of oats should be one-half the initial price for wheat. Unless there is a fair relationship between these initial prices the farmer is going to have a hard time determining what to seed because he has no way of knowing what the final payments are likely to be.
We are not at all sure that we will have adequate markets for our grain. At the present time our wheat market depends to a large extent upon United States dollars being made available to Great Britain for the purchase of Canadian wheat. There is no assurance that those dollars will continue to be made available. Despite all that was said by ministers of the government during the election, that the C.C.F. were talking more blue ruin and that there was not going to be a trade crisis, we found that just a few weeks after the election there was a real trade crisis. Great Britain announced that she would be cutting her purchases in the dollar area by 25 per cent. That was important to Canada. A British dollar crisis means a Canadian trade crisis. When Great Britain is short of dollars then the Canadian farmer may well face a market crisis in the not distant future.
Britain has been entering into bilateral trade agreements with many countries. Up to the present she has signed almost forty such agreements and has established sources of supplies of food outside the dollar countries and outside of Canada. The permanent loss of the British market will mean serious difficulties for Canadian agriculture. We are facing difficulty in marketing cheese, in marketing apples, and we have large stocks of evaporated milk on hand. I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to check the figures I am going to give because I believe they are right.
As of October 1, 1947, we had on hand 16-4 million pounds of evaporated milk; on the same date this year we had on hand 56-6 million pounds, an increase of 40-2 million pounds. We have stocks of butter amounting to approximately 70 million pounds. It would be nice if we could sell our butter surplus to Great Britain, but we are not likely to be able to do that. Great Britain has bilateral agreements with other countries for the purchase of butter. She had a contract with Denmark for the year ending September 30, 1949, for the importation of 130 million pounds. Denmark has agreed to deliver to Great Britain 75 per cent of her butter surplus up to a maximum of 330 million pounds per year. If we had the chance to ship to Great Britain only a

small fraction of the butter that she is buying from Denmark under a bilateral agreement there would be no talk of a butter surplus in Canada.
We are not just losing, we have already lost the British market for a great many of our agricultural products. I admit that the British market has been reasonably good for wheat and cheese, although there is some talk of difficulty in getting a cheese contract for 1950 of the same size and at the same price. But let us consider our bacon exports to Great Britain, and the figures I give are taken from the dominion bureau of statistics publications. Exports of bacon sides and hams in the first eight months of 1947 to Great Britain amounted to 168-6 million pounds; for the same period this year the exports amounted to 28 million pounds, a drop of 83-4 per cent.
Was that from a lack of contracts?

No, that was from a lack of government policy. The farmers of western Canada will produce 160 million pounds of bacon for Great Britain if the government will establish contracts over a period of years instead of from one year to the next, and leading to one crisis after another. In that same period in 1947 we shipped 8-8 million pounds of dried eggs to Great Britain; in the same period this year we shipped 3-8 million pounds, a decrease of 56-8 per cent.
Was that from a lack of contracts?

I suppose that will be a periodic question. Our farmers are willing to produce bacon and eggs and milk and apples and almost any other commodity for Great Britain if they can be assured of a market year in and year out. The policy this government has followed has brought about a reduction in the British market to the point where our farmers have entirely lost confidence.
Is it not true that the socialist government in Great Britain have not been able to finance the purchase of our goods?

In my opinion, we have lost our markets in consequence of the policies followed by this government and the United States government, and not because of the policy followed by the British government. I should like to go on and quote more statistics to show how this government has maintained our British market, and I can tell hon. members opposite that the figures get worse instead of better.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
Our exports of shell eggs in 1947 amounted to 29-7 million dozen; in the same period this year we exported 8-7 million dozen, a drop of 70-7 per cent.
Why?
We have a surplus of milk in Canada at the present time. Our exports of whole milk powder to Great Britain in 1947 amounted to 232,000 pounds; this year we shipped exactly nothing.
Why?
A drop of 100 per cent.
Why?
I could tell the hon. member for Fraser Valley but I do not think he is capable of understanding.
Maybe not, but why?
In 1947 we shipped 16-9 million pounds of evaporated milk, while this year we shipped no evaporated milk at all, another drop of 100 per cent.
Again why?
I tell my hon. friend that in 1947 we shipped 16-3 million pounds of salmon; this year we shipped 922,000 pounds, a drop of 94-4 per cent.
Again why?
In 1947 we shipped 448,000 barrels of apples to Great Britain, and this year we shipped not one barrel, a drop of 100 per cent.
Again why?

Our shipments of dried apples to Great Britain dropped 100 per cent. Our shipments of canned apples dropped from 11-3 million pounds in 1947 to 2-6 million pounds in 1949, a drop of 76-8 per cent. We shipped to Great Britain in 1947 2-6 million bushels of potatoes, and this year we shipped no potatoes in that period, a drop of 100 per cent.
Why?
In 1947 we shipped 12 million pounds of poultry, and in the same period this year we did not ship any.
Why?

I do not mind how much noise hon. members make on the other side of the house. These are cold statistics, and I would

Supply-Trade and Commerce ask my Liberal friends from the province of Saskatchewan if they do not think that is a serious drop in the British market. I should like to read a press report of a statement by the Minister of Agriculture, which is to be found in the Leader-Post of June 24, 1949. The article reads:
"There is no evidence to support the contention of M. J. Coldwell, C.C.F. leader, that Canada is losing the British -market for food," Agriculture Minister Gardiner said here Thursday night.
The Minister of Agriculture said we are not losing the British market. If we take the average drop in the last two years for all these commodities with which I have dealt, we have lost the British market to the extent of more than 90 per cent.
Why?
I might ask hon. members opposite why, since the Minister of Agriculture said that we are not losing the British market.
Remember New Zealand.
What did New Zealand do?

The British people have not wanted to reduce their purchases in Canada, and they have only reduced them because they are short of dollars. They have proceeded to negotiate bilateral trade agreements with many countries. While their purchases of bacon in Canada have dropped precipitously in the last two years, nevertheless in the last ten days the British Labour government was able to announce an increase in the bacon ration from three to four ounces per week.
Election.

Because they have been
developing other sources of supply.
Denmark.

This year they have proceeded to get 20 million pounds from the Netherlands, 40 million pounds from Eire, 40 million pounds from Poland and 100 million pounds from Denmark, a total of 200 million pounds.
It is not a joke.

It was not a joke to the hog producers of western Canada when they found hog prices from August until September, a period of four weeks, dropped by $4 a hundred. You cannot blame that drop on the British government.
Oh, oh.
Whom are you going to blame it on?
I blame it on Canada Packers and some of the other packing companies.
What a joke!

I am sure there is no employee of the British Labour government buying hogs in the province of Saskatchewan. In that province, as in every other province, there is just the packing industry, which is controlled by a few large corporations.
What has that got to do with it?

Let us look at the British purchases of eggs. In spite of the fact Mr. Strachey has announced that Great Britain may not renew the egg contract with Canada, the British are not going without eggs. This year they have bilateral agreements for the purchase of 21 million dozen eggs from the Netherlands, 13-5 million dozen from Poland, and 81-3 million dozen eggs from Denmark, a total of 115-8 million dozen eggs. We would like to have the British egg contract renewed, but whether or not it is, Great Britain has been able to develop other sources of supply.
Will the hon. member permit a question?

In spite of the interruptions, the fact remains that Canada is facing serious marketing problems.

Hon. members of the house may laugh if they want to. I do not mind, but the farmers of western Canada do not think that the present market prospects for agricultural products are a laughing matter.
Hear, hear.

I should like to suggest to the government that it undertake a different

policy. I was hopeful, from a statement the Minister of Trade and Commerce made this afternoon, that perhaps the government would make some changes in its trade policy. If I understood him correctly, he said that a better bilateral balance of trade would mean a better over-all balance of trade. In other words, if our exports to and our imports from the United States, and our exports to and imports from the United Kingdom are more nearly balanced, it will be a good thing for world trade. I suggest to him as a positive measure that he should do for the government of Great Britain exactly what he is asking that government to do for Canadians. Our government is asking the government of Great Britain to sign bilateral agreements for the purchase of Canadian agricultural products. I suggest that we as a nation should be prepared to sign bilateral agreements with Great Britain for the importation of British manufactured products. I can tell the minister that in western Canada there is an organization which I believe might be of some help to the government in this regard. I refer to Canadian Co-operative Implements Limited.
We have a huge market for agricultural implements in western Canada, and at the present time a great percentage of them must be imported from the United States. If we could change our imports of agricultural implements from the United States to Great Britain, I believe it would not only help Great Britain to solve her dollar problem but would also help our agricultural producers to maintain the British market. I believe if this government would sit down with officials of the British government and officers of Canadian Co-operative Implements Limited arrangements might be made under which a considerable quantity of British agricultural implements could be brought to Canada and sold by C.C.I.L. throughout the western provinces. Our farmers are interested in purchasing British implements, because they believe that to be to their own advantage; and I believe everything possible should be done to facilitate the importation and distribution of such implements.
We have all read the statement the Minister of Agriculture made to the FAO conference at Washington. The minister realizes that Canada, together with other major exporting nations, is likely to be facing agricultural surpluses in the near future. Such references are made time and again throughout his speech; but while eighty per cent of his remarks dealt with the surpluses that may be imminent, he had very little in the way of concrete proposals to remedy the situation. I know the FAO proposals may have their shortcomings; but I believe any international
Supply-Trade and Commerce arrangement which would enable us to get rid of our surplus products should receive the full support of this government. So, if other nations agree, I hope this government will be prepared to advance its share of the money required by the FAO for the purchase of agricultural surpluses.
If the government does not do any of these things, and even if it does, I believe there is need for a further extension of price support legislation. If we do not get another egg contract with Britain our poultry producers are going to need assistance through a price support arrangement. The Saskatoon Star-Phoenix reports that within the last two weeks the price of grade A eggs in that city has dropped by 11 cents a dozen. So I say that if we do not get an egg contract with Great Britain the government should support the price of eggs in order that our poultry producers may be assured at least a minimum standard of living.

I thank the committee for this indulgence, and I shall be through in a moment. I was just saying I believe it is of great importance that the government should establish price support legislation for the most important agricultural commodities. If there had been a guaranteed price for bacon at the local delivery points we would not have seen a_$4 drop in the price of grade A hogs within the period of a few weeks.
Since we are experiencing difficulty in selling many of our agricultural products, and probably will continue to experience that difficulty, and since the government have not taken the necessary steps to move our agricultural surpluses to the hungry people of the world, I suggest there is something else they might do that would be of great benefit to the Canadian people. I believe there is a place, in respect to certain commodities, for what I might term a consumption subsidy. We have large stocks of milk and butter on hand. We may have great difficulty selling our eggs before very long. These are protective, highly nutritious foods, and certainly it is in the best interest of our nation that Canadians should consume as much butter, eggs, cheese and milk as possible year in and year out. At the same time, in the interests of agriculture it is necessary to have adequate support prices; and a consumption subsidy would permit people especially in the lower income groups to make increased purchases of those commodities and at the same time guarantee our farmers a decent income.
At the present time we see huge surpluses of farm commodities looming on the horizon. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has said that a better bilateral balance of international trade would help world trade, but the fact is that the government has not taken adequate steps to bring about that balance. So I hope that the government will now take the necessary steps to increase our purchases of British products so that a market for Canadian timber, fish and agricultural products may continue to exist in the United Kingdom throughout the years to come.

Mr. Speaker, trade, the subject which is engaging the attention of the committee at the moment, is of the highest importance to all Canadians. The prosperity of Canadian agriculture is a matter of concern not simply to the Canadian farmer but to everyone in this country. The strength and buoyancy of our exports are likewise matters of concern to all Canadians. There is no country the wide world over whose people have a greater interest per capita in the maintenance of export trade than Canada. It has been said times without number that one out of every three Canadians-sometimes it is put as high as three out of every eight- depend directly upon the exports of this country for their livelihood and employment; and in passing it might be observed that of the other two-thirds a goodly number depend for their livelihood upon the purchasing power of the one-third who owe their employment directly to our export trade. I add, Mr. Chairman, that this is not a new situation. It has always been so in Canada.
I begin with this general observation, sir, that the approach of all thinking Canadians, the approach of this House of Commons, and the approach of the government to this subject should be characterized by a sense of realism. The time has long gone by when this House of Commons, or the Canadian people, are going to be cajoled into a sense of unending security by bland statements from the Minister of Trade and Commerce at Ottawa. We who have heard statements from the present Minister of Trade and Commerce in times past will be on our guard against easy optimism.
The country was on its guard, too.
What country?
The country was on its guard during the recent elections.

I am going to have something to say about the recent election, Mr. Chairman, and the way in which some ministers were responsible for the Canadian people forming conclusions that were not based upon facts. I am not referring only to the deliberate suppression of reports oh the part of the government that the Canadian people ought to have had, although that was a factor. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, of course, played a leading part in that act of suppression.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order; that statement is out of order.

The same Minister of Trade and Commerce played a leading part in

certain statements in reference to the trading position of this country, which I propose to mention now.
I begin with an incident that occurred in this house on April 25 last. At page 2520 of Hansard, you will find a statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in reply to a question. It reads as follows:
The present state of our markets in the United Kingdom is quite normal.
It was on that statement, a statement that could not possibly be made to harmonize with the facts, and on similar statements during the campaign that the minister and his associates won the election.
It is a good statement.

A good statement? It is a statement that cannot be harmonized with the facts. If a good statement is one that serves the purposes of the government, regardless of the facts, no matter how far that statement flies in the teeth of the facts, then of course it was a good statement. It served well the partisan interests of this government but, sir, it did the greatest violence to the facts. It was not a matter of more than three weeks-
Our wheat is all gone, anyway.
Your wheat is all gone, anyway? If the hon. gentleman is interested in wheat, I am prepared to tell him it is high time he worried about the wheat markets of this country.
I am not a bit worried.

The hon. member is not worried. There is a typical remark coming from a government supporter. Is it any wonder that this gentleman, and others of his political stripe, are not worried when they hear airy statements from the ministers opposite, which are intended to create a sense of optimism but which do not fit the facts.
A few weeks after the Minister of Trade and Commerce made this extraordinary statement in the House of Commons on April 25, I heard the minister's opposite number in the government of the United Kingdom, the Right Hon. Harold Wilson, president of the British board of trade, make a comment in the city of Toronto on the state of Anglo-Canadian trade. This was the very thing the Minister of Trade and Commerce was talking about on April 25, when he said that the state of our markets in the United Kingdom was quite normal. What did Mr. Wilson say? These are his words:
We have reached a critical situation in Anglo-Canadian trade.
Mr. Wilson did not make that statement merely in this country, but on his return to
Supply-Trade and Commerce the United Kingdom he delivered a radio broadcast on Anglo-Canadian trade. In the course of that broadcast, he made this statement:
Nineteen forty-nine is a year of crisis in our trading relations with our sister country across the water.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce said there was no crisis, yet within a couple of weeks thereafter the president of the British board of trade says Anglo-Canadian trade has reached a critical condition, and that 1949 is a year of crisis.
Labour government.
Yes, and what about this government?
Good government.

It was a party to telling the people of Canada that there was no crisis when, in fact, there was a crisis of emergent proportions, sir. Hon. members opposite know well that, by some strange coincidence, there were emphatic denials right up until June 27, from the Minister of Trade and Commerce and others of his political ilk opposite, about the existence of a trade crisis in the United Kingdom.
What did the people say?

It was not more than 48 hours later, that the full impact of the crisis was exposed to the view of the Canadian people. You will remember that it was only a matter of two or three days after June 27 that the British government made its announcement of the forthcoming drastic curtailment of imports from Canada. There may be some gullible members, sir, following the government in this house. There must be a good deal of gullibility, if you take the sum total on the government benches; but is there any one of them, sir, who is gullible enough to believe that that trade crisis was created after June 27? They know quite well, sir, that the trade crisis was existent throughout the spring and the election campaign, but this government managed-as it did in connection with other matters-to suppress it until after June 27.
It will be remembered that Sir Stafford Cripps made this announcement in the early days after June 27. I refer to a comment by an official of the Department of Trade and Commerce in Ottawa on July 15 concerning that announcement, which is reported as follows:
He estimated on the basis of Sir Stafford Cripps' announcement in London cutting the United Kingdom's 1949 dollar purchases by 25 per cent, Canada would lose by $60 million to $80 million this year. "If the slashes continue, then next year-1950-will be the crucial year,'' the official said. A continued

Supply-Trade and Commerce 25 per cent cut next year in Canadian exports to the United Kingdom would mean the loss of more than $100 million.
You will remember, sir, that the full purport of the statement by Sir Stafford Cripps was that the reduction of purchases from Canada and the United States, which he found it necessary to make, amounted to no less than $400 million per annum. This is a matter that no Canadian dare contemplate without the gravest misgiving. I say, therefore, sir, that this whole question must be approached, not in the airy sense of optimism and jaunty complacency of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but with adequate knowledge of the hard realities of the situation-for hard realities there are in this trading situation facing Canada. It is of the most momentous concern to all Canadians.
Sir, it is in that spirit of realism that I approach this problem, not in the spirit of unwarranted optimism, and certainly not in a spirit of unwarranted pessimism, because I am a great believer in the future of this country. I take second place to no man in my faith in the future of my country; but I think it is the first duty of every Canadian who loves his country to be a realist in appraising the strength of the forces that' confront Canada today. Among her trading problems-
And holding up pipe-line legislation.

He would be very happy if the minds of the people of Canada could dwell away back two or three years ago when the trading situation of this country was not nearly so serious as it is today. I am concerned about the situation today, and I wish the minister were more concerned about it, or more candid in voicing his concern about it.
The unfavourable trading deficit with all non-commonwealth countries in 1948 was $149 million; in 1949, it is $317 million. Our favourable balance with all countries in 1948 was $225 million; in 1949, $72 million. I think the most significant figures among those that I have just read are first of all the increase in our trading deficit with the United States. It has risen in the first nine months of this year compared with the first nine months of 1948 by $163 million. It rose from $283 million to $446 million. That in itself presents a problem of staggering proportions. And, sir, our position with the United States in respect of trade is a problem that must engage the attention of this house as it is

engaging the attention of those in Canada who have been studying the outlook for our foreign trade.
These figures alone do not tell the whole story, because while to commonwealth countries we shipped more than we purchased from them to the extent of $389 million, our deficit on trading account with non-commonwealth countries was $317 million. This favourable balance, sir, to which I have referred, of $72 million in the first nine months of this year is significant not alone in the fact that it represents a very substantial reduction as compared with 1948-actually it is less than one-third of our surplus on commodity trading account in 1948. But, sir, let us also consider how the purchases of the commonwealth countries-I am speaking now particularly of the United Kingdom- are being financed at the present time.
Thanks to the European recovery plan there is in these figures of purchases by commonwealth countries from Canada a total of $293 million in round figures, all provided out of funds supplied by the United States. That represents in itself practically our whole :rading surplus with the United Kingdom. In other words, our favourable trading position vith the United Kingdom is due entirely to ;he European recovery plan financed by the Jnited States. How long we may expect that ;o continue no man dare prophesy, but the noment it is withdrawn, as we can see from ;hese figures, immediately our trading sur-alus with the United Kingdom vanishes.

Supply-Trade and Commerce are on the basis of inflated dollars. And we should remind ourselves more directly than did the minister in his remarks this afternoon. These figures do not represent volume increases in proportion at all. I should like to quote a paragraph to the house from the October issue of the Canadian Statistical Review at page 5, where it states:
The value of gross national product, according to an estimate recently published by the bureau-
That is, the dominion bureau of statistics- -was $15,450 million in the year 1948. This is 137 per cent above the $13,591 million for the year 1947 which, in turn, was 13-8 per cent higher than the
1946	figure of $11,936 million. Price rises were more influential than volume in these increases.
