What are the policies of governments abroad? What are the policies particularly of our two principal fellow-traders, the United Kingdom and the United States? Their policies are of the most direct interest to all Canadians. The policies of the United Kingdom government, whatever may be the circumstances facing that government which in their view justify the course they are taking, are nevertheless policies that must fill us all in this country with grave misgivings as to the future of our markets in that land.
I have already referred to the drastic curtailment of imports from Canada which was announced by Sir Stafford Cripps just after the election in this country. What has happened since? We have seen the United Kingdom government announce devaluation -a very drastic devaluation which necessarily makes it more difficult for the United Kingdom to purchase from Canada because their pounds are exchangeable for fewer dollars to purchase our products.
That was one factor. But there are other factors in the situation. One of these is the policy of bilateral agreements which the socialist government in Great Britain is pursuing. It is true they have expressed regret in doing so, but the fact remains that they have been pursuing policies of bilateral trade which are harmful to Canadian interests. Canadians would do well to remember that the commodities that are the subject

Supply-Trade and Commerce of these bilateral trade agreements are in many cases commodities that we in Canada are producing and would gladly sell to Great Britain.
Let us remember that three years ago this country had twenty-three contracts with Great Britain for the sale of food to that country. Yet today we have only four, three of which expire at the end of this year. Our wheat contract expires next July.
In 1948 United Kingdom purchases from Russia increased by $79 million, her purchases from Poland by $30 million, her purchases from Hungary by $15 million, her purchases from Denmark by $61 million, while at the same time her purchases from Canada fell by $67 million. Can Canadians sit back and contemplate this situation with any measure of equanimity? Dare the government contemplate that situation and remain idle in the face of it, or refrain from pursuing more effective measures than they have been following?
It is with the greatest regret that I find it necessary to comment upon some observations made by socialists in the United Kingdom concerning purchases from Canada. Unfortunately these utterances have been increasing in number in recent months. It was in September last that Mr. Wyatt, a socialist member of the United Kingdom parliament, undertook to say in the House of Commons at Westminster that the United Kingdom was paying for Canada's dollar deficit in international trade. He told his people that the United Kingdom parliament should insist upon Canada accepting payment in sterling for her sales to the United Kingdom. Presumably he meant blocked sterling. Other socialist members in the old land have taken up the cry, and similar statements have been emanating from socialist members of parliament at Westminster from time to time since. Those statements however reached a sort of climax when probably the most radical member in the cabinet of the United Kingdom, the Right Hon. Aneurin Bevan, undertook only a month ago to say, during a debate at Westminster on the subject of devaluation, that if the United Kingdom stopped buying from Canada-and I am quoting his words-"what is a British financial crisis would become a Canadian crisis".
With all due respect to the sources from which those statements come, I think it is well that some should remember-and I am sure no Canadian likes to refer to these facts -that Canada has sought to be generous in her trading relationship with the United Kingdom during and since the war. Our Canadian wheat farmers have accepted prices

under the wheat agreement which were substantially below the price brought by wheat on the world market. We have made substantial gifts and have provided substantial loans to the old land.
We do not mention these things in any invidious or carping spirit. We say this only in the hope that those who are responsible for shaping the trading policies in the old land today will bear in mind that Canada has sought to do her part to rehabilitate the trading ability of the old land. At the same time we ask those who are shaping those policies in the United Kingdom to remember what Canadian food producers strove to do for the British market during and since the war, and that it would be a betrayal of the Canadian food producer to close the door to the entry of Canadian food products into the United Kingdom today. That is a fair attitude for Canada to take in trading approaches to the United Kingdom, and it should be recognized as of first importance in shaping the policies of the Canadian government.
This parliament would like to know the outcome of the conference held in the United Kingdom in October in which the deputy minister of trade and commerce and the deputy minister of agriculture participated. We want assurances that the Canadian food producer is not going to lose that market which he has served so well. We would like to know what steps are being actively pursued at the present time to preserve that market for the Canadian food producer.
An amendment was introduced by this party on a recent occasion-I am not going to refer to the debate-which asked this government to pursue steps to bring about a conference of commonwealth countries to consider trade. That proposal was rejected by this house. But another opportunity is offering. There is to be a meeting of ministers of the commonwealth countries in Colombo, Ceylon, in January. When his department's estimates were being discussed in the standing committee on external affairs recently I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs if trade matters would be discussed. His answer was that po decision had been reached about the discussion of trade matters. I urge upon the government that there is nothing more important which that conference could take up, no subject of more lively concern to the whole commonwealth and certainly to this country, than our trading relations with the commonwealth countries.
The situation is fraught with the gravest dangers for Canada if we continue to place more and more of our trading eggs in the United States basket and fewer and fewer in

the baskets of the commonwealth countries. Warnings have not been lacking. Warnings have been offered to the government by those to whom the government should have been glad to listen. Months ago the Canadian Exporters Association made a submission to the Minister of Trade and Commerce containing this statement:
Since the beginning of this year the foreign sales representatives of our member firms have reported a very serious drop in sales in their long-established British empire markets. This falling-off of export sales, in many cases right down to zero, is so alarming-
That was months ago.
-that the association deems it advisable to bring the matter to the immediate attention of your department.
Urgency is the keynote of that statement. Here is another statement in the same submission, and I remind you that this was made to the minister months ago:
Canada finds herself today in the peculiar situation, as the sole member of the British commonwealth unable to trade more or less freely in empire markets, which have become increasingly important to Canada in the development of her world trade. Canadian firms have spent a great deal of effort and huge sums of money to develop markets in these countries. They have become dependent upon these markets for a considerable part of their production and many thousands of Canadians have relied upon them for their livelihood. Unless some action is taken with alacrity Canadian exporters feel that they might be faced with the permanent loss of the empire markets, which would inevitably mean distress and unemployment in Canada. As a matter of fact, some of our members already report that it has been necessary to lay off some employees because of the present unfavourable situation in sterling area markets.
The Canadian Exporters Association went on to say that they feared unemployment was beginning among the dock workers at Halifax and Saint John; today we are seeing Canadian bottoms sitting idle in those Canadian ports. Today's issue of the Ottawa Journal contains a dispatch from Pembroke stating that the dollar shortage will force the Canadian Splint and Lumber Corporation, one of Pembroke's largest industries, to close on December 16, because of the British dollar shortage.
So far as our trading relationships with the United States are concerned, we will not forget that this government stood by passively and watched the flight of dollars to the United States in the long months before November, 1947, when they finally moved to put into effect their austerity program. The same Minister of Trade and Commerce who sits opposite tonight in his airy, optimistic way said that those restrictions would be in effect only a matter of months. When he was asked later what he meant by months, he proceeded to tell the house that that meant a year. The fact is that those restrictions have already been in effect for over two years and we have
Supply-Trade and Commerce no indication that the government proposes to demobilize them. The indications are that they will be intensified because of the existing situation.
I wish there were time to develop some of the thoughts I had hoped to bring out at this time, but as I have but five minutes left I should like to point out the danger of counting on the United States as a market for our exportable surpluses and the danger o'f trifling with the growing loss of our markets in the United Kingdom. So far as our markets in the United Kingdom are concerned, I remind the committee that for the past 80 years goods having a high labour content have predominated in Canadian exports to other British markets. At the same time Canadian exports to the United States have consisted uniformly of goods of low labour content. In 1946, 77 per cent of Canadian exports to the United States had a low-job value, while at the same time 85 per cent of Canadian exports to the sterling area were in the high labour-content category. In this way the sterling area provided direct employment for approximately 1,250,000 Canadians, while the United States provided employment for probably one-fifth of that number.
My concluding remarks will be in the form of a warning of the danger of relying, as we are today, on United States markets, and I ask the committee to bear these facts in mind.
1.	The Canadian and United States economies are similar and, therefore, competitive. They are not complementary, and therefore there can be no thought of integration of the Canadian economy with that of the United States. That would be fraught with the greatest economic and political danger for all Canadians.
2.	The United States cannot purchase the goods and services formerly taken by the sterling area except in the particular circumstances of very great world-wide shortages which would allow them to sell abroad their own surpluses of the same materials.
3.	The United States soon will be in the position of having unsaleable surpluses on the domestic market in nearly all lines. United States productive capacity has increased an average of 60 per cent in ten years while its population has increased only 12 per cent.
4.	The United States cannot increase the purchases of the materials which she does take from Canada on a scale sufficient to compensate Canada for the loss of employment in the industries exporting to the sterling area. If the United States were to double the purchases made in Canada in 1948 and if we were at the same time to lose all

Supply-Trade and Commerce our sterling area markets, Canada would be left with unemployed that some have estimated might come close to one million.
5.	Integration would end all reason for the maintenance of the vast majority of the United States branch plants in Canada which now have a capital value of over $2,000 million.
6.	"Integration", therefore, would be accompanied by a de-industrialization of Canada and the emigration of profession and industrial classes.
7.	If "integration" were finally completed, Canada would be left with a primary-products economy which would be required permanently to maintain a position similar to that of the United States of seventy-five years ago.
The situation is fraught with the greatest danger. What is needed on the part of the government is a sense of realism, of candour, of honesty with the Canadian people, and above all a sense of pressing urgency.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be very brief. Strange to say, I agree with something the hon. member for Eglinton has said. The only difference between myself and the hon. member for Eglinton is that I do not feel capable of speaking for forty minutes every day on each subject that comes before -the house. I do not feel that I have a knowledge of all subjects that come before the house, but apparently he does. I do not have the privilege of speaking for the minister, but I can speak for the private members of British Columbia and say that we believe in the hon. member for Eglinton's argument as to a trading balance. We believe that where you want to sell you must be willing to buy. I want to bring to the attention of the hon. member for Eglinton, and of the people of Ontario, the fact that he came out to the province of British Columbia and tried to sell-
When?
Prior to the 27th of June.
Nobody bought.

They were not willing to buy. I want to say to the hon. member for Eglinton that in each and every riding where he spoke in the province of British Columbia the Liberal doubled his majority. I am informed the same form of salesmanship took place in Ontario. I do not want to delay matters, but when the hon. member for Eglinton has what I would call the audacity to criticize the policy of this government, with the mandate it received in his own province on the 27th of June, I think he has gone one step too far. So far as I am

concerned, I will be delighted to contest my riding or his any day that he wants to ride on the record of the present government.

I rise on a question of privilege. The Minister of Trade and Commerce disputed the carryover figures I gave in relation to wheat. I want to say to him that those figures came from the Canadian Coarse Grains Quarterly Review of August, 1949, published under the authority of the hon. gentleman, and the figures are to be found on page 9. The paragraph containing them reads:
With the exception of barley, stocks of Canadian grains in all positions at July 31, 1949, were well above the totals at the end of the 1947-48 crop year. Total stocks of Canadian wheat at the end of the 1948-49 crop year were 98-7 million bushels, an increase of 21-0 million over the July 31, 1948, revised carryover total of 77-7 million bushels.

I do not intend to speak at any length, but there are a few points I want to deal with concerning our international trade problems. There is no doubt that today a great deal of concern is being felt by people in different parts of Canada as to the international trade situation. Statements made by responsible ministers of the crown and officials add to that fear and increase the confusion in the minds of the people regarding our problems and their solution. I want to congratulate the hon. member for Assiniboia upon the very constructive speech he made in dealing with these problems. I noticed that hon. members opposite did not seem to appreciate his speech, and I want to point out to them that they cannot hope to laugh off a problem. You cannot find a solution by laughing it off.
Statements appearing in the press at the present time show that once again, as in the 1930's, we see on the one hand surpluses of goods piling up and on the other hand masses of people starving for the want of those goods. I should like to quote one or two press dispatches. There is one in the Manitoba Co-operator which reads:
At the same time leading economists of member countries will wrestle with what FAO director general N. E. Dodd describes as the "terrible paradox" which finds farmers in some lands threatened with ruin by plenty while millions in other lands are oppressed by hunger and poverty.
Then again:
On one side of the gap stand consumers, many of them desperately hungry, eager to have more of the things they need, eager to earn more to pay for them as fast as they can. On the other side stand producers, afraid that if they produce as they can and would like, they may drown themselves in unsold surpluses.
I also think the speech made by the Minister of Agriculture before the 5th session of the FAO conference on November 24 should be carefully read by all members. I

congratulated the Minister of Agriculture upon a speech that he made before the Canadian chamber of commerce in London, England, in December, 1948. I thought it was a very fine speech. I only regret that he did not make a similar kind of speech during the election campaign. I must admit I helped him out by quoting it quite profusely in my constituency. Again he has made what I consider to be another fine speech, and again I say it is a pity the speech he made before FAO was not made during the June election campaign. I want to quote briefly from the speech, starting on page 1, and reading as follows:
The review of the world food situation prepared by the council of FAO presents a disturbing picture. Parts of it, in fact, must raise the question in the minds of many as to whether FAO's goal of a better nourished world is likely to be realized, at least in the foreseeable future. The picture presented in that report shows that, while total world agricultural production has regained pre-war levels, it has not kept up with increasing world population, and that the supplies available per person are still below pre-war levels. Even more serious, however, is the tact that although production gains by countries are unevenly distributed, monetary difficulties are threatening to prevent freedom of movement of foods and other necessary products from "surplus" to "deficit" areas. This, in turn, might easily lead to a slackening of the productive effort in some countries and an increase in cost which may deny food to the people of other countries.
Further down:
This threat of accumulating food supplies in some parts of the world while people in other parts of the world are underfed must evoke unpleasant memories in many of us . . . Our monetary difficulties today threaten to reproduce the situation which existed twenty years ago, a lack of that free movement of food from those with food to spare to those in want. And unless some way can be found of solving this problem we cannot hope for that "all-out" effort by exporting countries that is needed if the people of the whole world are to be adequately fed. In other words, it is difficult to persuade a farmer to produce more food for the hungry in some other land if he sees no likelihood of its ever getting to the people who need it-if, in short, it is likely to remain on his hands.
Further on there are these words:
Unless a concerted effort is made to restore trade and payments equilibrium, the persistence of present difficulties threatens to reverse the trend towards freedom from want. It would compel some of the largest surplus producing countries to restrict their agricultural output and deficit countries to expand their production at any cost.
It seems to me that is the great danger at the present time. In spite of the fact that the production of food is insufficient to meet the needs of the world today, surpluses are starting to pile up already; and of course, as the Minister of Agriculture points out, if surpluses start to pile up in a great producing nation the producers of that nation are bound to begin to curtail production. No
Supply-Trade and Commerce industry can continue to expand its production unless it has an expanding market. If it did it would simply mean that it would be headed for bankruptcy.
I do not think anyone would try to argue that farmers in Canada today are making an all-out effort to expand production. No one could reasonably expect them to do so, because they have no assurance that in future they will have a market for their production at reasonable prices. Then statements made by the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and by the FAO tend to put a doubt in the mind of the farmer as to whether or not he can afford to expand his production, because no farmer is going to increase production in order to create a surplus which will force down the price of his commodity. But as long as we have starving people in the world, as we are told there are today, there can be no justification for reducing production; and it would be an act of criminal folly on the part of any government to encourage any lessening of the production of food while at the same time there are starving masses of people in various parts of the world.
As my reason for saying the farmers have grounds for fear that their markets may be limited, let me quote one or two press dispatches. First I refer to a Reuters dispatch of last month:
British bacon imports from Canada in 1950 will depend on the dollar situation and on the volume of goods and services Britain can sell for Canadian dollars, food minister Strachey told parliament yesterday . . .
At Ottawa it was learned that the Canadian government already has been informed that the United Kingdom will buy less bacon from Canada in 1950 than she did in 1949.
Statements like that appear day after day in the Canadian press. I quote another:
The British chancellor of the exchequer told a London press conference that Britain is considering switching over to European sources of supply for some of the foodstuffs she formerly purchased from Canada. He specifically mentioned eggs.
Then in the Wheat Pool Budget of November 8 I find this statement:
John Strachey, British minister of food, in the course of a speech made at Coventry, England, stated that the British government may reduce its purchases of wheat from Canada after July 31, 1950. He is reported to have said the reason therefor is that Britain cannot buy with dollars it hasn't got.
Whether or not we agree with those statements we must recognize that as long as these statements continually appear in the press they are bound to have a depressing effect upon agriculture; and when the Minister of Agriculture makes such a statement as he delivered before the FAO conference it is bound to give rise to a great deal of concern. I want to congratulate the

Supply-Trade and Commerce Minister of Trade and Commerce on the speech he made recently before the export association at Montreal, in the course of which he clearly pointed out Canada's international trade problem. I quote from his statement, as it appeared in the Montreal Gazette:
If Canada, without further loans, is to hold her current trade status with Britain after the termination of Marshall plan aid in 1952, then Canada must increase purchases from that country by an annual $365 million.
That is approximately the trade balance in Canada's favour. In the year ended last September, Canada bought from Britain $325 million worth of goods and sold $691 million.
Then further down:
On the other hand Canada's balance was adversely affected by trade with the U.S. While Canada shipped $1,550 million worth of goods in the same twelve-month period, she imported about $2 billion. The $450 million deficit was collected from the rest of the world through Marshall aid dollars.
"Obviously, our policy must be to export more to the U.S. or alternatively to buy less from that country.'1
I think the question people are interested in having answered is, just what is the government doing to bring about that balance, the need for which the minister pointed out? In that speech he went on to say that in Canada we have a shelf of projects under consideration by the government for the purpose of helping to maintain or build up effective demand in this country, but of course on the other hand we must realize that building up effective demand in this country will not provide a market for our wheat. Therefore we must be prepared to accept imports from other countries in payment for that wheat. Of course if we maintain a high effective demand in this country there will be a demand for the imports that can be brought here in exchange for our wheat. But, as the minister pointed out, we have something in the neighbourhood of another $365 million of imports we will have to bring in from Britain, before we establish a balance and we will either have to sell more to the United States or buy less from that country. That is one of the reasons we in this group have not opposed the idea of exporting oil and gas to the United States once our own needs are satisfied. We need dollars in the worst way, and certainly that would help relieve the difficult dollar situation we are now facing.
The point the government do not seem to appreciate is that the situation which has developed today is the inevitable consequence of the international trade and financial policies which they fostered immediately after the war. Time and again in 1944 and 1945 we of this group stressed the fact that if we wanted to sell to the nations of Europe we

must be prepared to accept payment in the currencies of the European countries, and then use that currency to buy their goods. Yet every time that matter came up in the house we had the minister of finance of that day insisting that when we exported to Europe we must be in a position to obtain dollars in payment, in order to meet our debts. Just let me quote from Hansard for April 11, 1946, at page 764. Mr. Ilsley said:
. . . we must be able to use the proceeds of our exports to the United Kingdom and the continent of Europe in paying our own bills and debts in the United States . . .
Then on April 16, 1946, at page 919, I asked this question:
Will Canada be prepared to accept goods from the United Kingdom in repayment of loans? How will the United Kingdom maintain convertibility of the pound if Canada and the United States do not provide the United Kingdom with dollars by purchasing British goods to the extent of the British credit?
Mr. Ilsley replied:
... it is not necessary that there should be adverse balance of payments as between Canada and the United Kingdom in order to enable the United Kingdom to repay the loan . . . She can pay for Canadian goods by exports to other countries as well as to Canada. Under a multilateral trading system and convertible currencies-[DOT]
If that is the solution, why do we not adopt it? If it is so simple that all you have to do is maintain a multilateral system and you can balance your trade, why after four years is this multilateral system not in operation? The government know very well that you cannot have a multilateral system of trading when you have an unbalance as between the dollar and sterling areas amounting to something in the neighbourhood of $6 billion; and it is nonsense to talk about the convertibility of currency as long as that situation exists. At that time the minister of finance was thinking in terms of those years before the war when Britain had large credits she could draw upon from India, Egypt and other countries. Those nations had surpluses in their dealings with the United States, and they paid their surplus dollars to Britain. Those days are gone. Today both India and Egypt are heavy creditor nations of Great Britain, so that actually Britain is having to pay pounds to those countries instead of receiving dollars. So it will be quite evident now, even if it was not evident to the government at the time, that the only solution is, as the Minister of Trade and Commerce said in Montreal, to expand our imports from Europe and, on the other hand, to either sell more to the United States or buy less from the United States to make up our deficits with that country.
Now, the Marshall plan has been helping to balance international payments for the last few years, but the Marshall plan ends

in 1952. Everyone is wondering what may happen after 1952. ECA reports that Europe will not be in a position to balance her trade by then; she will still face large deficits. We are being warned now by the European nations that they will have to drastically reduce imports from this country, not because they want to, not because they do not desire our goods, but simply because they have not the dollars to pay us. Just so long as we insist upon payment in dollars instead of accepting goods from those countries, they are bound to take that action.
I was somewhat interested in a statement that appeared in the Wall Street Journal of November 18 as to what will likely be the successor of the Marshall plan. If this proposal is put in operation, then I believe Canada will be facing an even more serious situation than she is facing at the moment. The article reads as follows:
Aim to finance over million tons of grains, tobacco, cotton and fruit yearly.
The state and agricultural department are evolving a large scheme to get rid of America's mounting farm surplus by shipping them abroad at a loss . . .
Barter U.S. commodities would be traded at cut price valuation for foreign, strategic material. Permission to do thus has already been voted by congress.
Under this proposal private exporters would sell certain over-plentiful commodities abroad, accepting payment in foreign money. The U.S. government would then give the exporters dollars for his alien paper.
I point out, Mr. Chairman, that if the United States does that, and we refuse to do likewise, then we are going to be left holding the bag. This group has been advocating that plan for the last five years. We have insisted that, if we are really interested in putting international trade upon a sound basis, then we must be prepared to accept payment in the currency of the importing nation. That would be absolutely justified, because international trade is the exchange of goods. The only thing we need with which to buy European goods is their currency. If we really intend making international trade what it should be, we do not need to get dollars from Europe; we can accept their currency and buy their goods with it. Then there will be no difficulty in balancing our trade with Europe, and Europe will not have to curtail purchases from this country because she has not got dollars.
The former minister of finance would have argued that we must receive dollars to meet our deficit with the United States. I would say it is not the responsibility of Europe to make up our deficit with the United States. It may be argued that there is a large dollar content in the goods we ship to 45781-164
Supply-Trade and Commerce Europe, but there is also a large dollar content in the goods that Europe ships to Canada, because Europe has to buy a great deal of raw material from the United States. The one would balance the other. I would say it is our obligation. At Montreal, the Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed out that was the situation, that we would have to balance our trade unilaterally with the sterling area and unilaterally with the dollar area. In the future, we could not expect to get dollars from Europe to make up our deficit with the United States.
I only wish the government had recognized that fact back in 1944-45 because, had they done so, they would not have been so keen on signing international monetary agreements such as the Bretton Woods agreement, and the non-discrimination clause in the Geneva trade agreements. I am not attacking the Geneva trade agreement as a whole, but I do strongly attack that so-called non-discrimination policy which denies a nation the right to determine its own source of supply.
In this group, we have always felt that international trade should represent a reciprocal, and mutually agreeable, exchange of goods and services between nations; not an exchange of goods for money. Hence, creditor nations must, in the future, be prepared to accept goods and services in exchange for credits held by them in other countries. We feel that, until such a system has been adopted, nations must have the right to determine their source of supply for imports, in order to protect their own balance of payments. We also oppose any attempt to bring about the free convertibility of currencies, or the adoption of the gold standard.
In order that a balance of international payments may be achieved, we advocate the following procedure: An exporting country should accept payment in credits in the importing country, which it would have to clear directly or indirectly, by purchasing that country's goods or services. If it failed to do this, then under a statute of limitations, any credits still outstanding after a specified period would be cancelled. It is interesting to note that that suggestion, that a statute of limitations should be invoked, has been made by the London chamber of commerce, a body of men who have probably had more experience in international trade than any other body in the world.
It is interesting to note also that Maynard Keynes, in his original proposals, recognized the need for some method of forcing a creditor nation to accept payment in goods, or alternatively to forfeit the payment of those

Supply-Trade and Commerce credits. We feel that this will make international trade an exchange of goods and services, and will place the responsibility for achieving a balance upon both parties trading together. I know that many people will argue that a system of trading of that kind would be bilateral and, therefore, undesirable. It would be a simple thing, however, to put that on a multilateral basis by establishing an international exchange upon which credits held in one country could be traded for credits in another.
We feel that this trading should be executed at a fixed rate of exchange, based upon the relative value of the currencies as determined by their purchasing power internally. For example, if this country exported a million dollars' worth of goods to Britain and only needed half a million dollars' worth of goods back, we could then trade that half million dollars' worth of goods through the international exchange to France for half a million dollars' worth of goods from that country. Then, France would accept the goods we had coming from Britain, and that would put the trading on a multilateral basis. It would be an exchange of exports for imports instead of the currency of the exporting nation. In that way, it would be a comparatively simple matter to maintain a balance of trade.
Any nation that refused to accept imports in exchange for the credits it had established would be making a gift to that nation because, if over a period of time they refused to accept imports, under a statute of limitations that credit would be wiped out. That was one of the main arguments we had against the Bret-ton Woods agreement; it had a strong procreditor bias. It placed the full responsibility for balancing trade upon the debtor nation instead of placing it equally upon the creditor and debtor nation. If a proposal such as I have outlined were adopted, it would be placing pressure upon the creditor nation as well as upon the debtor.
I noticed that the Minister of Agriculture refers to the proposals put forth by the FAO in his speech delivered before that organization. At page 5 he says:
Canada, therefore, is prepared to give serious consideration to any international action designed to attain production and distribution of food. From this point of view we are interested in the proposal advanced by the director-general for an international commodity clearing house. While endorsing the principle underlying this proposal we are not in agreement with the means which, it has been suggested, are necessary to reach the objectives.
Then, the minister concludes with these words:
In conclusion, we in Canada agree with the United States and the United Kingdom that suggestions

should be considered by a working committee. The Canadian delegation will co-operate in every possible way on such a committee.
We hope that out of this conference will come a suggestion that we can all agree on.
It is very unfortunate that so far nothing has come out of that conference. There were proposals for setting up a world pool of food in order to get food from surplus countries to needy countries, but as the Minister of Agriculture said, in so far as Canada was concerned, they were not prepared to agree to the proposal. There was one very interesting feature in the proposal, namely, that surplus food could be sold from that pool to countries and payment accepted in their own currency. I look upon that as a forward step, and there does seem to be a growing recognition of the fact that if we want to expand international trade we must make it an exchange of goods to the mutual advantage of all, and therefore be willing to accept payment of our exports in the currency of the importing nation. We have had that suggestion from the London chamber of commerce of Great Britain. According to the Wall Street Journal that is going to be done by the United States after the end of Marshall aid. The FAO are suggesting such a proposal. Therefore I would urge upon the government that they give careful consideration to that suggestion because if after Marshall aid ends the United States exports her surpluses and receives payment in part in the currency of the European nations she will take markets away from Canada and we are going to be left holding the bag. I hope the government will take action before the situation gets any worse.

For the information of the new members who may be bewildered by this debate I may say that opposition parties have been making these speeches since 1944 in every successive session, and if they will go back through Hansard they will find no change in the nature of the speeches.
An hen. Member: Nor in the attitude of the government.
Perhaps not.
And the government has learned nothing.
And our prophecies were borne out.

Just to bring the position of our trade with the United Kingdom into perspective let me give the committee the trade figures back over the years. Take the year 1929, the most prosperous year between the two wars: our exports to Britain in that year

were $290 million. Take the year 1933, which is perhaps the worst year in that period. Our exports to Britain were $210 million.
Marshall aid is helping now.

Never mind what is helping us now. Perhaps I can put these figures on Hansard without too much interruption. Take 1938, the most prosperous year in the thirties. Our exports to Britain were $339 million. In 1939 they were $328 million; in 1947, they were $751 million; in 1948, $686 million; and in 1949, which is not completed, they will be well over $650 million. This is the way in which we are losing our exports to the United Kingdom.
The minister will agree that Marshall aid is providing the dollars.
My hon. friend has the idea that we should go back to the primitive days and exchange goods instead of using money as a medium of exchange.
No. I said that we should accept the currency of the importing nation, which is a totally different thing.
The hon. member said a lot about, exchanging goods. Modern civilization has found that a good way to exchange goods-

Order. May I
remind hon. members that they must not interject or ask questions of an hon. member who has the floor unless they first obtain his consent.

Mr. Chairman, so much for the over-all situation. Judging from these figures I have quoted one would hardly reason that we are losing our trade with Britain. Let us take the individual commodities. What about wheat? I think we are in grave danger of being oversold on wheat from this crop. After the first of the year the government s going to start advertising to farmers asking :hem to please deliver all the wheat they possibly can as early as they can for the balance of this crop year so that we can deliver that wheat on commitments already made.
What about oats and barley? There again our sales are getting ahead of deliveries, and we are rather worried that we may be getting into an oversold position on oats and barley. What about flax? An hon. member spoke of the great surplus of flax from last year. We did have an unusually heavy carryover. That flax is moving out, and we are just wondering whether we shall have enough flax to run us through the current year and take care of the export commitments.
45781-164^
Supply-Trade and Commerce
What about bacon? I am not too proud of our position in bacon. We contracted with Britain to furnish a quantity of bacon in the year 1949, and we are actually delivering a pretty small proportion of that contract. There are two sides to a contract. Some people may say that Canada is in a very happy position, but I do not think that the United Kingdom, which holds the other end of the contract, is so pleased with our deliveries on the bacon contract; and that also holds for the egg contract we made for 1949. That contract is still current, and we are still in a very serious deficit position in our delivery of eggs.
No one has said anything about beef. The beef prices in the Winnipeg livestock market reached the highest point within the last two or three weeks that they have reached for many years. Speak about other products. If there are large unsold surpluses I do not know what they are. But what is our trade position today? The Minister of Trade and Commerce cannot sell products that we have not got, and I do not know of any unsold surplus products that we have. Someone may mention dried milk. Perhaps we have dried milk. If we have an oversupply of dried milk, perhaps the remedy would be to sell milk in some other form which is readily saleable today.
We speak of butter, and compare the figures for butter this year and last year. The Department of Agriculture tells us that the stocks of butter on hand at the present time are just about enough to see us comfortably through the winter. May I remind hon. members who compare these figures with the figures of last year that last year we had to go abroad and import butter to carry us through last winter. That is the position of our exports today. Anyone who finds in them a great threat to the future of this country must view the situation with very jaundiced eyes indeed.
I hear hon. members speak of realism. Well, my experience with that phrase is that it is a synonym for pessimism. It is a great phrase used along St. James street and Bay street. The realistic view is always the pessimistic view. I am accused of being a great optimist, but I believe in making statements according to the facts which are laid before me. I have done that consistently and I have done it again this evening. I think that when next year rolls around and we look back upon the statements I have made tonight it will be found that they will be in just about the same position as they have been ever since 1944. In the past I think my predictions have been found to be fairly accurate.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

As a farmer I certainly hope that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is right in what he has just predicted. However, that is not the feeling that prevails in most rural areas in Canada. Certainly it is not the feeling out in Saskatchewan when just within the last month the price of eggs dropped 11 cents a dozen and the price of pork 4 cents a pound.
Was that drop due to a lack of outlets for the pork and the eggs? Was it not because the price of eggs got very far above the floor set by the British contracts, and the same with bacon?

A farmer out there is receiving at the present time about 28 cents a dozen for No. 1 eggs, and I do not think that is a price at which he can produce eggs at the present time. The minister gave certain figures with respect to our exports to Great Britain; I believe the figures were $648 million worth of exports. He did not point out that the price of those exports today as compared with the earlier period-in the twenties or thirties-is about twice as much. He did not give the volume. Certainly the volume is not as great now as it was then.
Let us look at the period between the two wars. We tried for years to build up our markets with Great Britain on pork products and dairy products. We established a grading system in this country for bacon. We established a grading system for our dairy products, and we tried to produce an article which would be acceptable to the British market. We tried to build continuity of supply for that market, because there are two things the British market demands: one is continuity of supply and the other is quality of the product.
We were reasonably successful. By 1939 we had built up a reasonably good market for cheese, bacon, apples, honey and certain other products of our farms and our fisheries. Then the war came along, and we found suddenly that that market was tremendously increased. We had become the only supplier. Encouraged by the government, the farmers of this country went into increased production so that they doubled and trebled their production of those agricultural products for the market in Great Britain.
I do not think anyone expected we were going to be able to maintain all of the market we had established during the war, or that we were going to be able to continue to supply the quantities we supplied during the war. But we did expect, and certainly the agricultural industry in this country had a right to expect, that we would retain at

least the major portion of that market. But when the war was over we found that the market slipped away from us.
Someone asks why. Liberal members across the way were shouting "why" only a few moments ago. The reason is perfectly obvious. When the war was over we found that the market we had created there had been created through loans we had made to Great Britain. We had given away a billion dollars' worth of our products produced in this country. When the war was over those loans were cut off. I do not think it was good policy to cut them off as quickly as the United States did-and we followed closely in her footsteps.
Great Britain had not the money with which to make purchases. She could have bought on a time basis, if we had been prepared to continue to give her credit. But, knowing well enough that she would never be able to repay those credits, she did the only honourable thing and tried to get in on a cash basis. She tried to get goods where she could exchange goods. But we refused to enter into a bilateral agreement with her on agricultural products.
It is only two months ago that our Prime Minister went down to the United States and speaking at Troy, I believe it was, he offered a bilateral agreement with the United States in the matter of arms-war materials. Surely if we can make a bilateral agreement for the purposes of war we should be able to make a bilateral agreement with Europe to feed the people. If we are going to have peace in the world, and if we are going to build a world which we can hope to improve and from which we hope to eliminate communism, then we had better get wise to ourselves.
I would suggest to my hon. friend that we have had bilateral agreements in bacon and eggs for several years-and for several years we have not lived up to our part of it.
We did not have a bilateral agreement; that was the trouble. What were we taking back from Great Britain? If we had been taking back goods from Britain we could have been exporting to Britain.
We had a bilateral agreement in which we agreed to exchange bacon and eggs for money. The money was forthcoming, but the bacon and eggs were not.

And why were they not? They were not because we never had any agricultural policy in this country under which the farmers had known for more than one year at a time what they were going to have to

produce. I am certain that if we had had contracts for a period of four or five or six years, with any feeling of security, on the part of those engaged in agriculture in this country, they would have produced the goods to meet that market. When they were told during the war that they would have a market at such and such a price for their goods, they produced the goods in this country; and we can continue to produce them.
Agriculture does not wish to shut down shop. We want to continue in production. Every farmer is anxious to produce. He does not like to see his buildings lying idle when he has spent hundreds of thousands of dollars to create those buildings. He would like to see them filled.
Why does he not fill them?

But so long as he has not the assurance of markets he is not going to produce. He is not just foolishly going to produce in abundance, knowing that if he does he will get no price for the thing he produces. That is what happened in the past.
I have here an editorial taken from the Rural Co-operator, and it says, "Must we farmers march on Ottawa again?" That is the feeling in rural areas of Ontario with respect to the marketing of our agricultural products. They say in this article that we should be exchanging our goods with Great Britain, giving her an opportunity to ship to this country.
I believe it was the hon. member for Fraser Valley who only a few moments ago asked a question about the price of goods that could be shipped to this country. Well, British tractors are selling here today for $200 to $400 less than our own tractors produced in this country. Someone may say, "Well, why are they not being shipped here? Why are we not buying more of them?" But to establish a market for tractors or farm machinery in this country you have to build up an outlet for that machinery. You have to build agencies to supply repair parts. No company will come to this country and spend millions of dollars to establish those agencies unless they have some security for a number of years. They will not come unless this government is prepared to guarantee that they will be protected in this market and that they will have long-term agreements.
If we want long-term agreements we can get them in Great Britain. Make no mistake about that. But let us remember that, as regards our markets in the United States for agricultural products, they are not worth the snap of a finger. If tomorrow the United States were to adopt the Brannan plan with respect to floor prices under agricultural
Supply-Trade and Commerce products, what would happen to us in Canada? Under the Brannan plan they propose to guarantee prices to their farmers according to the average price in the ten-year period from 1938 to 1948. Then they would put their agricultural products on the market and sell them at whatever they would bring. Our agricultural products going to the United States would sell, not at the floor price guaranteed to the American farmer, but at the competitive price at which those articles would sell on the American market. It would knock the bottom right out of the market in this country for agricultural products so quickly that we would be back to where we were in the thirties, and we would be back there inside of three or four years.
Those are the problems facing agriculture in this country. It is all right for the minister to get up and say that we have no problem, that they are not only Canada's problems, but that they are world problems. That is not good enough. It is not enough to say that because they are world problems we cannot do anything about them. That is what we said in the thirties. We said they were world problems and that we could not do anything about them. The result was that we went through ten years in which we sat here and starved in the midst of plenty, and the world starved.
This is just plain common sense. We have to meet our own problems. We cannot wait for the rest of the world to solve our problems for us. Our country must do something for itself. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has the ability; he is familiar with these problems. But I do not think he is justified in getting up and giving us such an optimistic story when he knows that conditions are serious, and that world trade today is in a serious condition. The minister knows that.
My hon. friend reads too many newspapers.

Well, perhaps I do read too many newspapers. Perhaps that is the only way the people of Canada can get their information-through the newspapers. And if we are wrong, then it is the press of this country, the minister says, that is to blame for the feeling of doubt in people's minds as to whether there are markets for all the agricultural products we can produce in the next few years.
He says we have a market for wheat. Yes, we have a market for wheat as long as the British agreement lasts and ECA funds last. When the world agreement comes into effect in 1950 and we have to sell our wheat to Europe and other countries for dollars, where are they going to get those dollars? They will be available only if by that time we are

Supply-Trade and Commerce buying sufficient of the goods they produce to supply them with dollars. Either that, or we shall have to make credits available to them.
I do not think these problems can be solved by any one method; a variety of methods will have to be used. We shall have to work along every possible line in order to try to solve these problems and create trading facilities throughout the world. I think the hon. member for Acadia outlined some good ideas in the speech he just made with respect to credits. I do not pretend to be a financial expert, but I do know something about conditions and I do know that in the world today there is a need of trade. I am sure the minister will agree with that.
We will not get that trade by being optimistic, by sitting down and saying that everything is lovely. The only way we will get it is by working at it. I think the minister would be doing a service to the country if he told us what was being done in an effort to solve the problems that face the world today so that those people who might be depressed will have a better idea of things as they exist and not just accept everything as being lovely. There is an old saying that everything is lovely and the goose hangs high. Unfortunately the farmers of Canada have been the goose and have been hanging high for too long and something will have to be done about it.

Mr. Chairman, the seriousness of the problem facing agriculture is almost beyond description. Back in the days of 1937 and 1938 we had just arrived at the position where we had a fairly decent market in Great Britain. As previous speakers have said, we had graded our products to the high standard that we thought the British people wanted. We were getting that business up to the point where we thought we were doing a good job.
When the war occurred everybody across the country thought that prices were going to go up, because that is what had happened in the previous war. The farmers prepared themselves to increase production, granted with some idea of making a little more money, but mainly to be patriotic and supply the food needed by our soldiers and by Great Britain. The farmers of this country were proud and happy to do that.
But what happened in 1941? At that time the government brought in its price control policy before farm prices had had a chance to rise to a level comparable with the rest
[Mr. Wright.3
of the economy. The prices of agricultural products were frozen at a low level. It was then found that in order to get production up to the point where we could supply a certain amount of food to Great Britain subsidies would have to be paid. Subsidies were necessary in order to encourage the production of more food in order to supply the hungry nations of the world. Production was increased accordingly to a point higher than it had ever been in the history of this country. Farmers were working with half the help they had before and producing twice the quantities of food. That just shows what can be done in this great nation when our farmers are encouraged to do it.
Then what happened? In 1946 and 1947 the subsidies were taken off, and the farmers were blamed for the increases that occurred in the prices of food. The consumer thought he was being gypped. He had become used to low food prices during the period of price control and when the subsidies were taken off the farmers were blamed for the increases that occurred.
There was a complete lack of foresight on the part of the government in not making contracts for more than one year and in not signing them until November or December. The farmers did not know what they were going to receive for their products until November or December in the year previous to the contract year. Did that make for increased production? I contend that it certainly did not. All the farmers had before them as an incentive to produce was a big question mark. They were given no encouragement. They were not told until the last minute what they were going to get for their products and production began to decrease because of this uncertainty.
Then in addition the farmers were being followed to the abattoirs, to the elevators and to the creameries by the income tax officials to find out what they were getting. Many farmers in the west had not been used to doing too many chores. Production was increased during the war by farmers increasing their hours of labour, but the time came when they began to stop working overtime to look after their pigs and other animals because no consideration was given for the long hours they worked on their income tax. They said they were not going to do that when they did not know what they were going to get for their produce, and the result was lowered production.
That is the position our farmers have been in for the last four years. No encouragement

was given to them. They were told that if they would take less than world prices for their agricultural products during the war, which most of them were happy to do, they would be guaranteed the English market after the war was over. We were guaranteed that by the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Actually those lower prices were paid in order to maintain the government's price control program. We took those lower prices on being promised that at the end of the war and following the war the contracts with England would be maintained at a reasonable level.
Have the farmers of Canada ever been as prosperous as they are at the present time in the whole history of Canada?
What has that got to do with it?

That is the same sort of question as was asked a few minutes ago when it was said that the farmers' income was higher than it had ever been in history. It was said that our exports are worth more in dollars than we have exported for years, but no mention has been made of the volume of exports. The value of goods today is practically three times what it was in those years. No wonder we are getting more money. But are we getting more net income? Of course not. There is a tremendous difference between gross and net income. It is more in gross income but the gross does not pay off the mortgage.

Then the hon.
gentleman-

What has happened as our production has gone down? England, in order to get enough food, was forced to make bilateral agreements with various other nations, even nations behind the iron curtain. She was forced to buy where she could sell her products. If we were able to supply England with as much bacon, for instance, as we supplied previous to the war, we would have maintained the bacon contract; but owing to the fact that the government
Supply-Trade and Commerce did not have the foresight to look ahead a few years, instead of just considering the situation at the moment, our production was allowed to decrease to a point where we could not supply what they wanted. England had to go elsewhere to get her food. There has been some controversy about the word "top-heavy" being in front of the word "surplus". Whether or not a surplus is top-heavy, it is a surplus, and if there is a surplus in the country then it is bound to affect the domestic price.
A surplus of what? What have we surplus? I should like to know about it so that I can sell it.
I ask the minister what these surpluses are.
You tell me what they are.
I do not need to tell you. I think you should know.
I do not know of any.

According to your own publications there are various surpluses, and I think probably it will be important to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce the question which I intend to do later on. As I said, there are surpluses, whether or not the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture think there are. The Minister of Trade and Commerce answered a question of mine the other day and said there were surpluses. Is he now going to say there are not?

I made a difference between surpluses over domestic requirements and unsold surpluses. I asked the hon. member which he meant, and I do not know yet. Perhaps he will tell me now. Which is it, a surplus over home requirements or unsold surpluses?
What is your definition of a surplus?
There are two definitions of "surplus".
What is your definition of a surplus?
I think my hon. friend is an artful dodger on that question.
I am asking you that question. What is your definition of "surplus"?

My definition of an unsold surplus is a surplus that remains unsold. My definition of a surplus in excess of domestic requirements is something quite different. If

Supply-Trade and Commerce my hon. friend will tell us which surplus he is talking about, we can follow him. I cannot follow him at all. I have been trying to make sense out of his remarks up to this point, and I have failed totally.
That is one man's opinion.
I think it is generally accepted.

I do not care whether or not the surplus is unsold. It is a surplus. How long are you going to hold it? What about the surplus of skim milk powder you are holding? Is that not a surplus? Are there not surpluses of apples?
I do not know of any.
Is there not a surplus of cheese?
No.
Why did the government buy 14 million pounds?
The government bought it because we needed a little aged cheese to sell in markets that were accustomed to being furnished with it.
Has that not been done previously?
Not for several years.
Have we not sold aged cheese to Great Britain?
Not in the last several years. We sell it right out of the creamery.

I think there has probably been quite a bit of aged cheese going to England in the last few years. I will say this much, that our cheese exports this year will be less than they have been at any time in the last fifty years, and a good deal less than they were in 1938 and 1939 just previous to the war. The same thing is true of bacon. I want to ask the minister a question now and I will be finished. I want to ask him to give us the export figures for various agricultural products in 1938 and 1939, and again in 1948 and 1949. I think the pre-war and post-war figures will provide a fair comparison. I think he will find in various instances the figures for 1948 and 1949 are less than they were in 1938 and 1939. I do not want dollar figures; I want volume figures. Until the government takes a much more serious attitude than apparently many members on the opposite side of the House of Commons took tonight, during a previous speech, when they apparently thought this was all very funny-

There were humorous
remarks and laughter from various places in the house; as a matter of fact I thought it was disgusting.
Get a soapbox.

I should like to have the minister give me the figures for the various agricultural products in the years 1938 and 1939, and particularly cheese and bacon, because they are two of the most important products, apart from wheat, that are exported to Great Britain. They are two of the products which we could export in sizable quantities to that country, especially cheese. The government has bought surpluses of some products and is holding them in storage, particularly powdered skim milk and butter.
We own no powdered skim milk.
I did not hear what the minister said.
I said we have no powdered skim milk.
Tell me how much powdered skim milk is being held in the country. You should have those figures.
I don't know.
What is this, a quiz?
Carried.
The minister should have those figures.
My hon. friend is making the speech. Why does he not get the figures? They are a matter of record. I have not the record here. If my hon. friend wants to use the figures he knows where to get them.
I have them upstairs.
Then why not use them?
I think it would be well to have the minister put them on the record. That is why I ask for them. If he cannot give us those figures now, I think he should get them.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. Perhaps we should not carry on this discussion. The minister can consider the request of the hon. member and give an answer later.

It is regrettable that the large numbers of members who were here

not so very long ago shouting "why" and "what are you going to do about it", have all disappeared. We are now probably getting to the time when we might find out something to do about it. In the first place, in a general sort of way it looks like the sheerest kind of common sense, if there is an abundance of goods in the world and an abundance of productive capacity, that it ought to be possible to let everybody enjoy some of that abundance. There must be a solution somewhere if only the person rises who has the idea what to do, and if only the rest of us will have sense enough to listen to him. There must be a solution somewhere.
There is something we can do about it beyond what we have been doing up to the present time. That ought to be obvious, especially when you bear in mind that the United States, for example, is deliberately planning to limit production on so wide and systematic a scale in respect of so many commodities by actual limitation of acreage in the coming year. Bearing that in mind while there are at least a billion people in the world on the verge of starvation, one must be struck with the fantastic grotesqueness of the whole situation. That ought to make everyone in this house and in every other legislative assembly rather humble about the matter, so that at least they would be prepared to listen.
This debate, I think, has taken a rather unexpected turn. We have been debating something we hardly expected to discuss under this item, but I am rather glad. I was just telling my seatmate that all the things I came here prepared to prove have been acknowledged, and what we have done is to go on from there.
I think the first thing it would be well to spend a moment on is this question of why we in Canada now have shortages in agricultural production, about which the two previous speakers had a good deal to say. At the risk of repeating some of their statements may I give what I think is the reason.
In the first place during the war, in 1943 and 1944, my constituency was literally covered with hogs. The people of my constituency can produce hogs today just as well as they did in 1943; and they are just as willing to produce them now as they were then. Why is it that you can hardly find a herd of hogs from one end of my constituency to the other today, whereas it swarmed with hogs in 1943? I should like the hon. member for Fraser Valley and some of those other smart boys over there on the Liberal side
Supply-Trade and Commerce to tell me why it is we do not find the hogs that we saw in 1943 and 1944. When they finish explaining that they will have the answers they were shouting for and laughing because they did not get. What was it that caused the hogs to be produced in 1943 and 1944? In the first place everyone was pretty certain there was going to be a tremendous demand for hogs for an indefinite number of years; they were reasonably sure of a market. Everyone was fairly certain that because of the war there would be a relative scarcity, and that prices would be reasonably good. The third point was that in 1943 and 1944 we had not learned that a government of the Dominion of Canada could be so unutterably stupid as to tax people for additional production. We actually had not had it forced upon our attention that you could get in charge of a country a group of men so completely lacking in intelligence as to do that very thing; so that if a man worked all day producing wheat, and spent two hours in the morning before going out to produce that wheat, in milking cows and taking care of chickens, and then spent two hours after his work producing wheat, to produce butter and eggs and hogs, the government would penalize him for performing that fine service. But we had that forced upon us by example after example, by stupid ministers of finance and national revenue standing up in this house year after year defending that sort of procedure and being rather proud of it.
Well, in those days we Social Crediters told them just what they were going to get; and they got it.
They finally convinced the people there was not a bit of use working overtime to milk twelve or fourteen cows; that all they would be doing was producing butter for Ilsley, or for Abbott, or for whoever happened to be finance minister in charge. Human nature is just about the same in this country as in England or the United States. No man is going to wear himself right out producing extra goods if he gets nothing in return.
By the way, I am only too happy to answer questions if I can hear them, but I would ask hon. members not to be so cowardly as to mutter them just loud enough so they can be heard by Hansard but not loud enough so I can hear and answer them.
I had not asked the hon. member a question, but I shall do so now. Were the farmers very much bothered with income tax back in the early thirties?

We did not have income tax in the early thirties. The trouble then

Supply-Trade and Commerce was that the more hogs and cattle you produced, the poorer you got. I will give the minister an actual example. My own family were in the business of producing beef and hogs. I grew up to that kind of thing; I am quite accustomed to it, and I know what it takes to make a little money. In 1932 one of my brothers came in and said, "We have sized up the whole situation as far as our year's work is concerned." At that time we had about 150 head of good cattle, pretty well bred Shorthorns. He went on to say, "We have made allowance for everything that goes into the production of cattle, and we are just $5 worse off for every cow we have on the range"; and all the cows had calves.
What was the reason for that? The reason then was that we were in a depression. We have not now got into a depression yet, but we are going to get into one if we keep on with the stupid practices in which we are engaging now. If that is done there will be a depression very soon; then we will have Liberals across the way asking, "Well, what caused it? What are you going to do about it?" Yet they will not listen when we try to tell them. That was why in 1930 people were not doing the very best that could have been done; but they were doing very well in my area, producing at a loss as long as they could stand it. I hope that answers the minister's question in that respect.
And now I come back to the question of why we are having shortages.
In the first place, we have had uncertain markets. In the second place, we have had uncertain prices. Then we have had an income tax structure that has penalized men for doing the things the country wanted them to do, that is, for producing hogs and milk and eggs and butter and all the other good things we needed. Those are the main reasons we now do not have the production.
We must recognize, of course, that we have nad some bad years. This year, for example, we had crop failures over a considerable area of the prairie provinces. We lost tremendously in the production of wheat and in many other lines of agriculture; but taking the country from coast to coast in a broad sort of way, generally speaking we could have produced pretty well, if only we had not discouraged our producers by utterly lunatic systems of finance.
That is the first thing. Now I think I shall pass from that aspect of the question after saying only this: If the government of Canada wants production it must do the things that any person fourteen years of age,


with common sense, would say should be done. That is, make it possible for a man to earn and keep a little money if he produces something extra. We have not had enough sense even to give a farmer an allowance for the work of his wife in milking cows, feeding chickens, and so on. We have not had enough sense even to make that provision under our income tax laws, so close have we come to the borderline of imbecility in following a financial course that is fantastic and incomprehensible.
Now I wish to turn to another aspect of the question. It has been well brought out in the quotations read by the hon. member for Acadia from the speech by the Minister of Agriculture at the FAO conference that the minister recognized that ours was a monetary problem. I wonder if the Minister of Trade and Commerce will recognize now that our problem is monetary. Will he recognize that our main problem is a monetary one, as his colleague the Minister of Agriculture said in speaking to the FAO conference? Will he recognize that the problem facing the world today is a dollar problem?
I will admit that the main obstacle to the kind of trading we would like to do is the inconvertibility of currency. Does that answer my hon. friend's question?

Very well; the convertibility of currency is a monetary problem, though fundamentally there are other considerations underlying it, such as the production and sale of goods and all that sort of thing. We need not go into those, though I believe I know them and could name them without trouble. The first thing for us to recognize in approaching this problem of international distribution, getting the goods that we can produce in such abundance on this continent into the hands of people on other continents who cannot produce abundantly, is that the fundamental problem is one of money.
Now then, what can we do about money? Where are we going to get the dollars? In order to point up the need for money, let us turn for a moment or two to what Canada did for Great Britain during the war. I am quoting figures which I believe are correct, because they appeared in the report of the Canadian Press from London dated November 26, giving the details of Sir Stafford Cripps' speech. In 1942, he says that Canada gave Great Britain a billion dollar gift. If we could give Great Britain a billion dollar gift during the war, why can we not give

her a billion dollars to help win the peace? We shall let any Liberal man who thinks he can answer that question think about it tonight, and answer it tomorrow. If we could give Great Britain a billion dollar gift during the war to help her buy our goods, is there any reason why we cannot give her a billion dollars today? If a billion dollar gift helped solve the problem of getting rid of our surplus goods during the war, then it is conceivable it would help to get rid of our surplus today.
In 1943 Sir Stafford Cripps says Canada gave Great Britain a $700 million interest-free loan, together with Canadian supplies valued at more than $2 billion. Then, after the war, we gave Great Britain a credit of $1,250 million. That is what we were doing to help Great Britain buy the goods we could produce during the war. Why is it that we have decided, now that peace is here, we cannot do anything like that? I invite every Liberal in this house to be ready to answer that question tomorrow. Why is it we have the idea we cannot advance loans like that to Great Britain any longer? We could do it when we were under the stress of war. It is a question that needs serious thought, and a serious answer.
If that was the way to solve the problem in war, then it is probably the way to solve the problem in peace. Immediately a question will be raised as to where all the dollars will come from. I do not want to become involved in a lengthy discussion, but before I make my next statement, I should like to say that the world is up against a crisis. The minister can be as optimistic as he wishes in the house-I do not blame him for being optimistic before the country. May I say that I have the highest regard for the minister. If there is any man in Canada who should be given the greatest measure of appreciation and gratitude, it is the Minister of Trade and Commerce. While I am on this little aside, I may say that if the Conservative members of this house want me to respect them, they will have to stop making insinuating and sneering comments against the Minister of Trade and Commerce. This man has done too many great things for this nation to have anyone make insinuations or slurs against him. I may say that anyone who wants to debate that question can get on the floor and I shall deal with him.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
A little while ago you said he was stupid.
Supply-Trade and Commerce

I am not saying that he was the one that was stupid; there are other people having to do with finance who just take the cake for stupidity at every turn they make.
While the minister can be optimistic just as much as he desires in the house, we should recognize that that is not the opinion held by people who are well-informed; who are not speaking politically or desiring to cheer up the country. I should like to refer hon. members to the interim commission of the international trade organization, reporting on the Geneva agreements on tariff and trade, signed in Geneva in 1947 by 23 nations. In a report called "Attack on trade barriers", it says:
World trade is today facing a crisis of perhaps unprecedented gravity. Even now, four years after the end of the war, there is no sign, of a restored equilibrium, and present indications point to a deepening of the unbalance and a sharpening of the issues involved.
Hon. members who are interested can get the Christian Science Monitor dated September 6, 1949, from the library and read that in an article entitled "Continued aid for Europe seen possibility until 1952". It is a Reuters dispatch from Geneva. I believe we can accept that as definite. Let us not try to put the picture in beautiful colours, but face the actual situation which confronts us. What are we going to do about this unbalance?
The only nations in the world who are in a position to do something about it are the "have" nations. Two of the greatest "have" nations in the world are Canada and the United States. I believe all hon. members will agree with me in that respect. If those two are the great "have" nations, then they have it within their power to do something about the dollar problem, while nations like Great Britain, Greece and Turkey are helpless to do anything really effective about it. It will rest upon us as an inescapable responsibility to do something about it. What are we going to do? Are we to sit here idly talking about our inability to take care of our own affairs, in a nation pouring out abundance, while letting less fortunate nations in the other parts of 'the world continue to suffer?
